NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS SUMMIT MEETING IN MEXICO-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, tomorrow, October 16, the citizens and governments of more than 100 nations, including Canada, will observe the first World Food Day, which will serve as a rallying point in the search for solutions to end world hunger and poverty. The natural right of all human beings to food was backed by the report of the Parliamentary Task Force on North-South Relations, which placed particular emphasis on food and agricultural production. The report was supported by all parties in the House, and its main thrusts were endorsed by the government.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras):
That this House affirms its desire that practical steps be discussed by the heads of state or government of 22 countries who will meet next week for the historic North-South summit in Mexico so that early progress can be made in negotiating the economic issues now dividing North from South and, further, that the text of this motion be sent to the governments of all 22 states.

Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Canadian veterans, those men and women who fought for this country, have to wait an average of 46 months to have their pension applications processed, and many will wait over five years. The War Amputations Association has been forced to take legal action against the Canadian Pension Commission to overcome the bureaucratic blockade. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said yesterday in the House of Commons, small businesses, along with farmers, fishermen and home owners, are indeed suffering as a result of his government's callous and insensitive monetary policy. In an effort to rectify the situation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae):
That this House urge the Minister of Finance to direct Governor Bouey to lower interest rates to reflect the Canadian level of inflation immediately, extend the life of the Small Businesses Loans Act, increase tax credits for research and
development through to production, and increase small business deduction limits to $200,000 annually and to a $1 million lifetime limit.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since the government plans to increase postal rates by almost 100 per cent while service is deteriorating to the point where some deliveries travel at the rate of one mile a day, and since the first priority of the Post Office should be to restore some semblance of efficiency and confidence in its operations rather than forcing Canadians to pay exorbitant charges for first-class postage rates when they are receiving third-class service, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk (Mr. Bradley):
That the Liberal government adopt as its first priority quality of service and postpone any rate increases until such time as the quality of service has been brought to respectability.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In view of the fact that the minister inaugurated an investigation into the effects of urea formaldehyde foam insulation last June, could the minister explain what the findings of this commission have been, and when he intends to take action on its Findings?

October 15, 1981
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: INVESTIGATION OF UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I must inform the House that the investigation is still ongoing and should be completed sometime in November. As soon as I receive the report I will make it public and the government will naturally take the required action following its publication. In the meantime, I can tell the House that tests are now being performed in several Canadian homes in order to determine the extent of the problem, to reassure those whose concerns are unfounded, and also to provide advice to those whose health may be affected by this substance. Canadians are being kept abreast of the results of the tests. As soon as we have obtained a representative sample we will also make it public in order to shed as much light as possible on this whole issue.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister, if I could get his attention. During the course of the postal strike this summer I think perhaps all hon. members might agree that the dumbest comment uttered by any Canadian fell from the lips of the Postmaster General when he said:
I can't accept that businessmen have to rely on the Post Office to make a living. If they do, they better find other ways.
I ask the Prime Minister whether this statement reflects government policy and, if it does not, will he publicly rebuke the Postmaster General for exhibiting such insensitivity and ignorance on such an important subject?

I think that what I said was nothing but a plain truism, meaning that people cannot rely exclusively on the postal service during a strike. I am absolutely astounded by the way this statement was interpreted and blown all out of proportion. I surely am the first to recognize that the Post Office is absolutely important and vital to thousands of small businesses in Canada and that the impact of a strike may be greater for small businesses than for other sectors of the economy. But what I meant by that statement was that the business community had to use some degree of ingenuity in a strike situation rather than ask the government to legislate the employees back to work. subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-DISTRIBUTION OF DOCUMENTS TO MEMBERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege pertaining to an answer given to me in the House yesterday by the minister responsible for housing and repeated again today. The question of privilege concerns a very important document which outlines the crisis in housing in Canada today.
I want to say at the outset that the question of privilege, however, does not deal directly with the thousands who are going to lose their homes, as important as that is; nor does it deal with the problems of renters, as important as that is; nor does it deal with the thousands of people who have lost their jobs as a result of the cutbacks in housing, as important as that is. The question of privilege pertains to the fact that a document prepared by a minister of the Crown has been made available, not to other ministers of the Crown involved directly in cabinet work, for which there is a long-established tradi-
October 15, 1981

tion-even though we do not accept all of that tradition-of keeping such documents secret and private, but that a document, which we think contains information which every Canadian should have in his or her hands, has been made available to certain members of the House of Commons who are not ministers of the Crown and denied to other members of the House of Commons.
More specifically, I know that the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre), who is not in the cabinet, has had this document made available to him. My information is that it has been widely distributed to hon. members on the government side. Therefore, my question of privilege is that in terms of their rights members of the House of Commons ought not to be distinguished as to whether they sit to the left of Madam Speaker or to the right of Madam Speaker; every member of the House of Commons ought to have precisely the same rights.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. BROADBENT-DISTRIBUTION OF DOCUMENTS TO MEMBERS
speechtext:
I am sorry that I have to call the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) to order. This question of the distribution of certain documents to some hon. members and not to others has often been raised in the House as a question of privilege and, of course, hon. members will recall that I have had to rule that in those particular cases they were not prima facie cases of privilege.
I must remind the hon. member that, first, as the hon. minister has not quoted from the document, he is not required to table it in the House; it is also his responsibility to circulate certain documents to whom he wishes. That is entirely his responsibility. The Chair is not able to determine what documents are essential to a debate; that is the responsibility of the government.
This might be a legitimate complaint on the part of the hon. member, and he might bring it up on other occasions, but he certainly cannot raise it as a question of privilege. Therefore, I must rule that he does not have a question of privilege.

speakerposition: subtopic

subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. My point of order is to request of you, under Standing Order 67(8), that my very brief petition be read by the Clerk.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
The hon. member might request that. The report has been tabled, so I think that request is quite legitimate. However, the hon. member will know that he cannot have the petition read unless he has the unanimous consent of the House. Therefore I must ask the members of this House if they give their unanimous consent to having the petition presented by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) read in the House. Does the House give its unanimous consent to the request?
Petitions

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think that it would be a departure from the ordinary routine of business in the House. Therefore, we cannot give our consent to his suggestion because we indicated that a budget would be brought in within the next few weeks and that any debate of the kind suggested by the hon. member would tend to delay our proceedings and consequently some worth-while budget measures. We are thus unable to give the required consent for that reason.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS

subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a separate point of order, but under the same provision, Chapter XII, 67(8). I must say I was not suggesting that we have a debate as was outlined by the minister. I was simply asking that it be read. That was the permission I was seeking. Perhaps he misunderstood the question. I was asking simply for a reading of the material that had been brought forward.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: The minister did say that a reading would interrupt the normal business of the House and, therefore, he could not give his consent. As well, he understood from the hon. member that it was just a matter of having it read. He did not give his consent to that. Therefore, the hon. member does not have a point of order.

subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
My point of order relates to the next section, which reads:
-if it complain of some present personal grievance requiring an immediate remedy, the matter contained therein may be brought into immediate discussion.
The first request I was making, and which was rejected on the basis of unanimity, was for a reading. At this point I am asking for this because of the personal imminence of the situation. I can give a specific case where in fact a group of Canadians will lose their homes if this matter is not discussed now. It is imminent and significant that the matter be discussed at this moment on their personal need. That is the reason for the petition and why the petition should be discussed.
There is nothing in Standing Orders to suggest this cannot be discussed. Because of that and because of the concern expressed by the members of the House of Commons, I would now request that we have not a debate but a discussion of this subject matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
My understanding of the situation is that if the hon. member did not get consent for a simple reading of his petition, for reasons which I do not have to describe, obviously someone in the House felt it was not urgent or opportune to disrupt the normal business of the House in order to deal with what the hon. member has suggested the House

October 15, 1981
Petitions
should do. The logic of this situation is that if hon. members do not want the petition to be read, then obviously they will not want to discuss it.
I remind the hon. member that petitions in this House have not usually been discussed. The rule read by the hon. member I believe refers to a different meaning of the word "petition" from the one which is accepted within the confines of our rules. When petitions are tabled in the House, a report is made as to their form. They might be read by the Clerk upon request if there is unanimous consent.
The only precedent I can find with regard to some follow-up to a petition was in the case of Mr. Maclnnis where the petition was referred to a committee. It was not discussed in the House at the time the hon. member is now suggesting this one should be. I think I can resolve this matter quickly by asking the House if it gives its unanimous consent to discussing the petition or to some kind of follow-up to that petition. Does the House give its consent to the suggestion?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am just about to announce an opposition day for next Tuesday. That will give the hon. member the opportunity to raise any issue he wishes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: The hon. member not having unanimous consent, the matter has therefore been disposed of.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
On the point of order, Madam Speaker, I wish to quote from Beauchesne, page 213, citation 694:
While a member has clearly a right to ask that a petition be read, it is a privilege, like many others, subject to the approval of the House itself. In case of opposition, the Speaker will put the member's motion "that the petition be read", formally to the House.
Nowhere can I find that it requires unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
I quote from Beauchesne, citation 695, at page 213:
A petition having been presented, and being in order as to the form, may, with unanimous consent, be read by the Clerk, and may thereafter, with unanimous consent, be referred to a committee.
That is citation 695 of Beauchesne.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: On the same point of order, I would suggest that the member is not asking that it be read by the Clerk but that the member himself be allowed to read it, which is not what is referred to in 695 but rather what is referred to in 694.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: I have to remind the hon. member that he may be asking for that, but that provision does not exist under our rules. The only thing that can happen with a petition is that, with the unanimous consent of the House, it may be read by the Clerk, not by the hon. member. Other things may then happen if unanimous consent is given to the reading of the petition.

subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
On a point of order, Madam Speaker. You mentioned that the precedent that has been set is that petitions
have been read in the past and, second, that they have been referred. There is no precedent in this House of Commons relating to discussion, as is stated under section 67(8). This would be a new precedent. You in fact would be creating a precedent by this decision.
I would ask that you give this very careful consideration and perhaps reserve judgment. The discussion of petitions is the most basic and fundamental right of democracy; it was a right before democracy was even created. The right of petition being a pre-democratic right, that right of petition must be given full opportunity in this House of Commons. Therefore, I ask that you consider it very carefully because there is no precedent that I can see nor that you have quoted which relates to immediate discussion, or in fact to a full majority being required for that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. WENMAN-PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS
speechtext: I will not entertain any further discussion because I have already ruled on this question. There is no precedent where a petition has been discussed in this House. I go by the rules which do not tell me clearly that a petition can be discussed if certain things happen. There is no precedent that allows me to permit the hon. member to have his petition discussed. The procedure by which that can happen did not take place in this House. The hon. member did not get unanimous consent for the first part of that procedure. That is why I ruled that we could not pursue the hon. member's suggestion. We should close debate on this because I have already ruled on it and the precedents of the House are quite clear.

speakerposition: subtopic
President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the new House leader for the Progressive Conservatives (Mr. Nielsen) and to tell him that the House leader usually inquires on Thursdays about the business of the House. Since he no doubt forgot to do so today, allow me to briefly summarize the business of the House for the next days. First of all, today and tomorrow we will proceed with Bill C-48 dealing with oil and gas and the Canadianization of our oil industry. Consideration of this bill will extend into Monday. Next Tuesday will be an opposition day, after which we will resume debate at the report stage, and I do hope that we will complete third reading of Bill C-48 before next Thursday. This work schedule will be followed for now and in the future until further notice, and I am thinking in particular of the notice provided for in the House order for the conclusion of the constitutional debate. Should the government decide to use this order of the House to end the debate on the Constitution, it must give notice, and I want to make it clear that this notice could be given any time as of today. However, the normal order of business will be as I just
October 15, 1981

indicated and will not be changed unless the House is otherwise advised, which includes the possibility of the notice required under the agreement reached for the conclusion of the constitutional debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was intending to rise just before orders of the day were called, as I believe to be customary, to establish the routine business. In any event, it would have given the House the opportunity of proceeding more efficiently through the daily routine business without interruption. I wonder if it is going to be the intention of the government House leader to continue the practice of holding House leaders' meetings.
I was grateful to him last week when he called me about 45 minutes before his press conference to inform me of the business of the House for the remainder of this week. My colleague from Nepean-Carleton informed me that in the past it has been customary to hold regular House meetings on a weekly basis, with rare exception. I believe it would be desirable to continue that practice; however, perhaps the government has something else in mind as a result of the changes to my left as well as here. I would hope we could re-establish the custom of holding those meetings.
Perhaps that would do away with the necessity that faces me now of inquiring of the government House leader whether it is the intention to allot the remaining four opposition days, which I understand must be allotted before December, so that we may deal with them in an intelligent manner with the House leader for the New Democratic Party.
Secondly, in view of the reluctance of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Finance to provide members of the House with information as to the date of the budget, perhaps the House leader could be more forthcoming and inform members of the House when that budget date might be.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is no question of reinstating the practice of holding meetings of House leaders because this practice is still being followed. There is therefore no need to reinstate it. We did not meet this morning quite simply because there was no change from what I had mentioned to my hon. colleague on the telephone last week and because I wanted to confirm it for the benefit of the other members on both sides of the House. It is certainly most essential for us to meet as often as necessary, and I do not restrict this to one meeting a week. It has sometimes been necessary to meet several times a day, and this could happen again. We have had that experience not so long ago. However, it has also happened that we did not have to meet in over a week because the business of the House was not proceeding quickly enough. If we were to complete the debate of Bill C-48 sooner than expected, I would certainly hasten to call a meeting, even before next Thursday. If my learned colleague
Business of the House
tells me that we shall be voting at the report stage of Bill C-48 on Monday, I shall be happy to hold a meeting Monday evening to plan the next day's business. However, let us wait and see what happens, but the principle involved is very important: it is necessary for the House leaders of all parties to meet in harmony as often as need be to ensure the smooth running of this Parliament. This is the responsibility of the House leaders. I congratulate the House leader of the Progressive Conservative Party on showing concern and I can assure him of my full co-operation in this regard.
As concerns the date of the budget speech, it is of course up to the Minister of Finance to set it. I am not in a position to contradict the replies that he or the Prime Minister have already given about this matter. It seems that the minister will be able to bring down a budget probably at the end of this month or in early November. In any event, I want to point out that the order of business will be announced as early as possible after we learn what will happen and that the only thing which could delay any bill, including the budget bills and the budget itself, would be a change in priorities; but if this were the case, I can assure the hon. member that he would be so advised within the time limits provided under any agreement or our rules.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: I listened very carefully to the government House leader; however, he did not cover the point I raised with respect to the allotment of the remaining four opposition days. I suggest to him we should have an early meeting, because it is simply impossible to deal with a division of allotted days between ourselves and the other opposition party in the House if we are going to be given them piecemeal. We must have some foreknowledge of when they are going to be called so that we may deal with them. I wonder if he might cover that point.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is no established practice with regard to a formal meeting for the designation of allotted days. On the contrary, it is a prerogative of the government under Standing Order 18(2) to set the sequence of government business. And my colleague knows quite well that I cannot break away from tradition and undertake to seek the advice of hon. members opposite every time we want to designate an allotted day. However, I want to say in all fairness that if he wants to submit a list of convenient days, as his predecessor used to do, although I cannot promise to accept his suggestions, I can assure him that 1 will give them very serious consideration.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a couple of matters I would like to raise. First of all, I am happy to meet at any time. I recognize that members of the House are expected to be prepared to deal with any matter on the Order Paper at any time, but it is difficult to order one's own life when we know

October 15, 1981
Business of the House
we only have an understanding as to the business of the House until Tuesday of next week. More specifically, when the information was given out earlier this week on what we were going to deal with, the government House leader indicated we would go to Bill C-23 in the event we completed Bill C-48.
I would like specifically to ask whether or not it is still the intention of the government House leader to proceed to that piece of legislation immediately in the event we complete Bill C-48 by the end of next week. Failing that, I wonder if we might even get a hint as to the order of business that might be called for next week in order that we can alert people to be as prepared as possible and thereby expeditiously deal with the matters that are before us.
Before I sit down, Madam Speaker, I might say, in regard to my colleague for whom I am filling in temporarily, that his state of mind would be improved considerably if the government were to give serious thought to legislation dealing with widows' pensions. I am sure he would be back in the House forthwith, and happily, if he could see passed through all stages and given royal assent a bill which would improve in particular the lot of women in this society.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
1 also wish to take this opportunity to congratulate my hon. colleague on having assumed those important duties and to wish a speedy recovery to his predecessor. He has now asked what bill would be brought in if consideration of Bill C-48 was completed by next week. I cannot go back on what I said to him last week; on the contrary, however, if it should happen that we had to change the priority which I had indicated to him he would certainly be advised in due time. As for the business for next week, I gave a good indication a while ago in my reply to the House leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. However, if my colleague wants to have an idea of what we will be doing in the following weeks, and that seems to be the intention of his question, I will remind him that we are still in the same session that followed two elections held in less than a year and that there is still a backlog of bills on the Order Paper.
Up to now we have passed 65 bills but there are still about 20 on the Order Paper and each of them is important. We would like to dispose of them before Christmas. There is also the budget debate coming up; and as a result of the budget some bills will have to be considered and also of course that major bill on oil and gas now under consideration. Essentially this is our calendar up to Christmas and I hope that we will make sufficient progress to enable us to begin 1982 with a new session, but I cannot at this time make such a commitment. However, I wish to assure my two colleagues that we will meet as often as necessary and, of course, starting next week.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want to ask a question with respect to the responsibility within the ministry for a certain statute. As my hon. friend knows, Bill C-43 dealing with freedom of information is before the committee in the name of the previous secretary of state. There is now a new Secretary of State; in the recent shuffle, the Minister of Labour has become the Secretary of State. The minister who had joint responsibilities for that portfolio and that of communications is now the Minister of Communications. Could the House leader indicate who will be responsible for the conduct of the legislation through the House, namely, the legislation known as freedom of information?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, according to the latest information, the minister who has piloted the bill through the House so far will continue to do so; should technical alterations in the bill be indicated, we will take what steps are necessary to obtain the required consent and make what changes are required. That is the gist of the information I was given; should I be mistaken, I shall see to it that the hon. member is advised accordingly as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker will remember that on a number of Thursday afternoons prior to the summer recess I asked the government House leader what intentions the government had with regard to responding to the fourth report of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. At that time the government House leader indicated that the government was working feverishly to come up with a response to the committee's fourth report, to the report of the select committee of the Economic Council, as well as to other proposals dealing with parliamentary reform. Now that the House has been reconvened, may I ask the minister whether he could indicate when this material will be put before the House?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
It is true that the reports mentioned by the hon. member do have a bearing on parliamentary reform generally and, more specifically, on the structure of committees. I have already indicated that we worked very hard on parliamentary reform during the last few weeks; we are still doing so. But the question remains as to whether or not the proposed reform should be negotiated with House leaders before the end of the current session or early in the next one. That is a matter on which I should appreciate the views of the hon. member and my other colleagues. In any event, I am not in a position to say today exactly when the proposed amendments and improvements to our Standing Orders will be brought in; that is, before the end of this session or early in the next one. That is something that will in all probability be determined in the next few weeks.
October 15, 1981

In the meantime, it is absolutely unthinkable that we should devote the time of the House, that is so precious, to a premature study of those reports which are doubtless important in themselves but which one way or another will be considered by the House or in committee within the framework of a reform of our Standing Orders.

Madam Speaker, it is the same point of order as that raised by the previous member regarding Motion No. 54 which I drafted. I drafted it with great care taking into account precisely the point that Your Honour raised. Citation 773(7) of Beauchesne reads as follows:
An amendment is out of order if it imposes a charge upon the public treasury-
I took great care in drafting the motion. The two points to which Your Honour referred were in relation to the formation of the compensation fund.
On today's Order Paper the motion reads, in part, as follows:
" 19.2(1 )(a) A compensation fund shall be established by the Minister of the Environment to provide for damages.
No cost is involved there. It goes on:
(b)	the compensation fund shall be funded by all persons who obtained an authorization under paragraph 3.2(1 )(b) by letters of credit totalling at least $500 million.
Funds are definitely mentioned in subclause (b) but they would be raised from the industry itself and the various corporations involved. There would be no direct charge under those letters of credit against the public treasury. The motion continues:
(c)(i) the compensation fund shall be administered by a board appointed by the minister and will be called the "Compensation Fund Board."
(ii)	in addition to federal officials the board referred to in (i) above shall consist of representatives from onshore and offshore fishing organizations, native groups, territorial and provincial governments, and industry.
Again, there would be no cost to the public treasury. That clause was discussed in committee and it was specifically drafted so that members of the board would be extracted from all those areas of the country-from provincial, municipal and territorial governments, native organizations and fishing organizations-and they would be voluntary members of the board. The costs of the necessary travel and so on necessary in
Canada Oil and Gas Act
order to participate in board activities would come out of the compensation fund itself and not the public treasury.
The other points raised in Motion No. 54 relate to the actual administration of the fund and the fact that the governor in council can make regulations to govern the administration of the fund. That would not cause any direct draw to be made on the public treasury.
With all respect to the Chair, I think it is clear that Motion No. 54 can be considered as an amendment that does not fall within citation 773(7) of Beauchesne. It is clearly something that can be debated. It is a viable amendment and, in my view, is certainly one of the most important components for the protection of the public interest in Bill C-48.

Mr. Speaker, we have a motion under discussion that, in effect, would provide for the establishment of a board to come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) and which would administer funds obtained from licence holders through letters of credit. I understand the argument from the hon. member opposite is to the effect that somehow this proposed amendment does not infringe upon the financial initiative of the Crown.
I would draw the attention of the hon. member and the House to page 182 of Beauchesne, citation 540, which reads in part as follows:
-an amendment infringes the financial initiative of the Crown not only if it increases the amount but also if it extends the objects and purposes, or relaxes the conditions and qualifications expressed in the communication by which the Crown has demanded or recommended a charge. And this standard is binding not only on private members but also on ministers whose only advantage is that, as advisers of the Crown, they can present new or supplementary estimates or secure the royal recommendation to new or supplementary resolutions.
The principle here is simply that the initiative with respect to financial expenditures must come from the Crown and the grant be made by Parliament. The reverse situation, one which the expenditure of money is recommended by Parliament and the Crown would concur, is impermissible.
Motion No. 54 sets out Clause 19.2( 1 )(d) as follows:
(d)	any person(s) claiming for damages may apply directly to the compensation fund-
Then it goes on:
(e)	the board shall review the case and make payment to the person filing the claim.
Accordingly, the amendment requires that payment might be made to all claimants. However, subclause 19.2( 1 )(f) provides that the compensation fund shall recover its award from the letter of credit. Thus there is always, initially, a charge on the Consolidated Revenue Fund under the scheme which may or may not, where no fault is found, be recoverable from the letters of credit.
In respect of two of the government's amendments to this bill, a revised royal recommendation has been obtained from the Crown on the advice of the responsible minister. However, this option is not available to a private member who does not

October 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
have any position as an adviser to the Crown. It can also be argued that the motion would extend the objects and purposes of the financial allocation in respect of the bill, since no such administrative body is contemplated under the present bill. It is an entirely new review system.
The current section of the bill which this scheme would replace provides a strict liability recovery without review, with recourse to the courts where damages incurred are in excess of the strict liability limit. This must of necessity be a much more limited system in terms of administrative cost than the amount proposed by the hon. member opposite. If the motion in fact infringes on the financial initiative of the Crown, I submit that no question can be heard upon it nor can an amendment to the royal recommendation be obtained on the initiative of the member.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on the intervention made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). I have looked at Motion No. 54 very carefully and my understanding of the motion conforms with that of the hon. member for Skeena, not with that of the parliamentary secretary. The pith and substance of the motion is not the establishment of any board, any modality or any instrumentality for the administration of the fund in question; the main thrust of the motion, as I understand it, is the establishment of a multimillion dollar compensation fund based not on money from the treasury, not from the federal government per se, but on letters of credit from parties actively involved in exploration or development on Crown lands.
In the case of environmental damage from such activities as exploration or development on Crown lands, compensation to affected individuals or groups would be awarded from funds based on the letter of credit of the individual operator found to be at fault. So the money does not come from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey), the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) or from the consolidated revenues of the Crown; it comes from a fund especially established for that purpose which would place a burden on people found at fault and in violation of the environment.
For that reason, I do not think the motion violates any parliamentary, governmental or political convention that this House must follow. I urge Your Honour to bow to the very strong argument made eloquently by the hon. member for Skeena and to favour his interpretation, which conforms with my own, rather than that of the parliamentary secretary.

I want to put it to Your Honour that the important point here is that the purpose of that section of the parliamentary procedure which denies to a private member the right to bring in a money bill deals directly with the power of the Crown to administer all matters of finance which require public expenditure. Mr. Speaker, yesterday, at the end of the day, I was half way through my speech on what were then seven environmental motions which would amend Bill C-48 at the report stage of Parliament's deliberation on the legislation. With Your Honour's indulgence, with the remaining time, I now wish to complete my remarks. All of those motions relate to Clause 80 of Bill C-48, concerning oil-spill type pollution from resource activities on Crown lands and standards for compensation to parties hurt by it. Motion No. 4, as I understand it, would actually amend Clause 2, not Clause 80, by adding a definition of "spill". The proposed definition would, I think, helpfully broaden what is considered a violation of the environment under the legislation.
Motion No. 51 would remove any distinction between an authorized and an unauthorized spill for the purpose of, for example, awarding damages to an offended party. To my mind, Motion No. 51 makes a lot of sense on the grounds that pollution is pollution whether the source is authorized or not. Moreover, damage to either the general environment or to a party's property is no less severe just because the cause is authorized.
My party and I welcome Motion No. 52, which would require that the proper authority be informed beforehand of any authorized pollution, and that the same authority, in turn, give immediate notice to the aboriginal peoples and others who may be harmed by the discharge. Perhaps such requirements will, for example, help the native peoples protect themselves against pollution from activities at their back door. At the very least, if I may say, these people will know what is being done to their habitat in the face of resource development in their area.
Motion No. 53 substantially clarifies the liability of anyone who has violated the environment under the terms of the bill. It does so by specifying that compensation must be paid when pollution impairs, for example, one's source of income through loss not only of personal property but also of the natural environment from which the income is produced. To my mind, this motion would make the bill much more sensitive to the particular circumstances of native peoples, who are often hurt more by the indirect effects of pollution than by its direct impact on their personal property. In my view, in the view of my party and I think in the view of others in the House, compensation should be paid in either instance.
I must confess that the import of the minor amendment-I think it is minor-proposed by the Minister of Energy in Motion No. 55 escapes me, so I shall reserve judgment until a fuller explanation is provided, perhaps by the parliamentary secretary who was in the House a few moments ago and who no doubt will be speaking later.
October 15, 1981

Certainly Motion No. 56 has my full support, for it rightly seeks to recognize in the bill itself that damage to the environment often becomes discernible long after the actual offence has been committed. Thus, any time limit on when a claim for compensation may be instituted must be sensitive to such situations. At present, Bill C-48 does not reflect that reality. I welcome Motion No. 56 because it attempts to redress the problem.
Motion No. 57 would require the minister to launch a public inquiry into any activity that violates the environment by the standards of the bill. As the legislation stands, the minister may initiate an inquiry, and I stress the words "may initiate". But he is not required to do so. In my view, the minister should be required to do so under specified conditions.
We have dealt with Motion No. 54 and I have expressed myself on that question. I regret that it was not included in the original grouping of the motions under debate now. Let me stress that the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee was very much in favour of the idea behind Motion No. 54. I think the motion as expressed and moved reflects pretty well the import of the representation made vigorously by CARC and it certainly reflects something of my own thinking on the question.
If I may conclude, the bill before us at the report stage will govern the way in which some $300 billion will be spent on the exploitation of energy resources on Crown lands in the next decade alone. Some $300 billion will be spent in the next ten years, but trillions of dollars will be spent by the end of the century. It is clear that the government intends to have only a tiny proportion of such large amounts devoted to the protection of the environment. That will be of as much concern to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) as it is to me.
Worse still is the government's decision to perpetuate in Bill C-48 its habit of entrusting environmental responsibilities, not to the Minister of the Environment, who I see in the House today, but rather to ministers whose principal preoccupation and mandate are the promotion of resource activities that pose the greatest threat to the environment. The resultant conflict of interest is so apparent that one is hard pressed not to assume it constitutes a deliberate effort on the part of the government to undermine the role and responsibilities of the Minister of the Environment himself.
If we do anything else today and in subsequent days in the context of these motions, it should be to redress that very serious problem which I think is more fundamental than the specific problems addressed in the motions themselves being discussed this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to speak in a debate in the House which concerns the north, however meaningless that debate may be in terms of substantive changes to the bill in question.
When I spoke in the House in December, I expressed some anxiety that northerners would be forced to pay all of the environmental costs of the non-renewable resource development which this bill intends to accelerate and that they would receive none of the benefits that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) intimates. I will talk about their concerns later in this debate in connection with the motions in question.
I would like first of all to talk specifically about the environmental aspects of this bill which affect northern people. My colleague the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) has already discussed the general inadequacies of the environmental regime proposed by this legislation. As far as northerners are concerned, the proposed amendments represent an absolute minimum of what is required to protect that land from irreparable environmental damage.
We have a large economic stake in the preservation of our environment and, on principle, should have much more input into environmental decisions affecting us. I do not think the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has ever really consulted people from the north in this regard.
I will address each of these motions individually. Motion No. 4 concerns the definition of an oil spill as "100 litres or more of oil or other foreign substance". This amendment is very important to northerners, as a huge oil spill would have
Canada Oil and Gas Act
disastrous consequences, as most hon. members know. That is obvious, but chronic dumping of small amounts can be just as damaging to the ecologically sensitive Arctic waters. Northern hunters and fishermen must be protected against gradual destruction of their source of livelihood. It does not matter whether marine fish and mammals are killed slowly or all at once; the result is the same and equally destructive to the traditional northern economy.
Motion No. 51 concerns compensation for authorized as well as unauthorized spills. There are two important principles at stake here which must be protected. One is that those who suffer the economic and social costs of environmental pollution must always be eligible for appropriate forms of compensation. The other principle is that those who cause such pollution must always be held responsible for their actions.
As the bill stands, people affected by oil spills fortunate enough to have the blessing of the government would not be eligible for such compensation. We think this is wrong. It will not matter to the people in the area of a spill if the pollution has government approval. The effect on the environment and on people's lives will be the same. To free the government from any liability in such cases, therefore, will be to deny people who are affected their basic rights. I urge my fellow members, therefore, to support our motion and thereby prevent the government from applying a double standard to the issue of compensation. And, I repeat, it does not matter whether oil spills are authorized or not. What matters is that people's rights to be compensated for the effects of environmental pollution must always be maintained without exception.
Motion No. 52 also concerns provisions for compensating spills. Specifically, it requires that authorized and unauthorized spills be reported to the chief conservation officer and that he in turn notify the peoples affected. In many ways this motion is a follow-up to the one I have just been discussing, since it tries to put into practice some of the principles I have already mentioned. If we agree that people should always have the right to be compensated for damage done to the environment on which their lives may depend, then it seems only reasonable that we also grant those people the right to know about the causes of that damage. In other words, if we grant them the right to claim damages, we must ensure that information about the sources of pollution is made available to them. Compensation provisions for peoples in the current bill may prove meaningless in many instances if reasonable notice of such spills is not given to the people who may be affected.
It should not be left to the aboriginal peoples to piece together, after the fact, where and when oil spills have occurred and who should be held responsible. To make the provisions for compensation effective the northern peoples will need ready access to information on the nature and source of any oil spills which may have affected their environment. It should be the responsibility of the government to see that this type of information is collected and made available to those people. The proposed Subsection 19(4) is designed to ensure that information on all types of oil spills is acquired by the

October 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
chief conservation officer. This would include both authorized and unauthorized spills.
The proposed Subsection 19(5) is intended to guarantee that information about all types of oil spills is communicated to those peoples who may be affected so that they may begin the process of obtaining appropriate compensation without undue delay.
Motion No. 53 refers to kinds of damages for which people may claim compensation. From the point of view of my constituents the bill as it stands is far too narrow in scope, which is something-if I may have the attention of the minister for a moment-I have not been able to communicate to the minister and his colleagues. It means that aboriginal peoples cannot claim for loss of their future incomes if these have been reduced by the effects of pollution. Furthermore, it means that people cannot claim for damages to property which is not privately owned. For instance, if a walrus herd or a fish run is seriously affected by an oil spill, then the people whose livelihood depends on them cannot seek compensation for the loss they suffer.
In this regard the people of the north are not even getting the same deal as east coast and west coast fishermen who, under Section 746 of the Canada Shipping Act, are allowed to recover for loss of income, including future income, resulting from damage to the fish stocks caused by pollution, even though their fish are not in privately owned water. And they are not getting the same deal as the aboriginal peoples in Alaska, who are eligible to receive compensation for any and all damage done to the lands "structures, fish, wildlife or other biotic of natural resources upon which they rely". This is a provision of the trans-Alaska pipeline authorization act of 1973.
The purpose of our proposed Section 19.2, therefore, is to ensure that people can receive compensation for all types of possible losses caused by oil spills and other types of pollution. This will include individual and collective losses as well as the loss of future income.
I would like to emphasize that the proposed amendment to Clause 49 of this bill does not ensure the adequate environmental protection which is urgently required for Canada lands. They are merely interim measures until a comprehensive regime can be put into place through appropriate legislation, which I advise the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) to introduce.
I note that Motion No. 34 has now been included in this group of motions, and I will speak to it. Motion No. 34 concerns one of the key environmental provisions of this bill. It deals with the environmental studies revolving fund. Bill C-48 as it is presently drafted divides the fund into two, giving discretionary power to both the Ministry of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Ministry of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Our motion calls for the establishment of a single fund under the Ministry of the Environment. Perhaps those two can start fighting.
While we see the value of government involvement in the resource sector, it is imperative that the government remove discretion on environmental studies from the departments which have the greatest interest in advancing the pace of development, namely, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
The amendments proposed in Motion No. 34 are based on the following principles. First, it must be clearly indicated that social as well as environmental considerations are covered by Clause 49 of this bill. Second, environmental and social studies and procedures in relation to Canada lands must be under the jurisdiction of the Minister of the Environment.
Proper environmental and social impact assessment and review procedures must be established. The present federal Environmental Assessment Review Process-EARP-is totally inadequate. The new procedures need not be established under Bill C-48, but the bill should at least contemplate such procedures as an integral part of the decision-making process.
Persons or groups directly affected by oil and gas activities under the act must be funded so as to enable them to participate effectively in the relevant environmental and social studies, public hearings and impact assessment procedures.
Interest holders, that is the oil and gas producers, should bear the cost of funding the environmental studies revolving fund and should fund, at least in part, those persons or groups affected by oil and gas activities in a prescribed region of Canada lands.
Advisory committees comprised of representatives from the oil and gas industry, public interest groups, aboriginal peoples and other groups or persons directly affected by oil and gas activities should be established from the prescribed regions within Canada lands.
Subclause (23) (a) of Clause 49 commits the government to discussions on environmental and social impact procedures. Considering the enormous impact of accelerated resource development in the north, it seems incredible that there is no legislated environmental impact assessment process in place. I advise the Minister of the Environment to get started on that. A comprehensive review of the existing procedures for assessing environmental and social impact is imperative in order to mitigate the negative effects of development in the north.
In the National Energy Program, the minister has stated that "our energy options are wide enough to preclude any sudden rush to energy choices that may compromise our social and environmental goals". His statement was a reaffirmation of the government's responsibility to inhabitants of the north and "the preservation of the peculiar ecological balance that now exists in water, ice and land areas in the Canadian Arctic". The government should demonstrate some consistency between what it says and what it does. Discussion of the environmental and social impact procedures is crucial to sound and responsible planning for northern development.
October 15, 1981

Subsection (23)(b) of our amendment in Motion No. 34 foresees the drafting of appropriate legislation following discussion of social and environmental impact procedures proposed in (23)(a). A precedent for such provisions is found in Section 2.5 of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement. Sincere discussions should lead to enlightened legislation on these matters.
Madam Speaker has suggested that Motion No. 54 is inadmissible. That is really unfortunate because for native northerners some sort of mechanism which would help them to obtain compensation without having to resort to costly court procedures would be most welcome.
Bill C-48 as it is presently drafted limits claims of liability to two years after the damage has occurred. This does not make much sense considering that some damages to the ecology are not immediately evident. The amendment suggested by the hon. member for Skeena in Motion No. 56 is much more reasonable in limiting the time for claims to two years after the damage costs or expenses occurred or became evident to the claimant.
If oil and gas activities in Canada lands results in death or injury or danger to public safety or the environment, we feel that the public has a right to know the facts. A public inquiry in these cases should be mandatory and not left to ministerial discretion.
I would like to conclude by repeating what should have already been made obvious over the past six months. Northerners are not happy with Bill C-48, with perhaps the exception of my hon. friend from Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). They were not consulted on the contents of the bill before it was introduced and they have legitimate fears about accelerated oil and gas activity on their lands. They will shoulder the burden of the serious and inevitable negative consequences of exploration and development and they still have no guarantee that they will have any of the benefits.
Environmental protection is one of the northerner's deepest concerns because when boom-and-bust non-renewable resource development has passed them by and when southern resource developers have abandoned their operations taking the resources and profits with them, northerners will still have to find a way to make a living from a scarred and radically altered land. Therefore, as the bill stands, without any of these amendments it cannot be supported.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to stand today and speak on Bill C-48, particularly Motions Nos. 4, 51, 52, 53, 55, 56, 57 and now No. 34, all dealing with the environment. I put forth the proposition that the window dressing it gives to the protection of the environment is just that.
I would like to refer to the remarks of the minister who spoke just a few moments ago. He said that the government had spent a great deal of time describing and defending the bill. I agree. That is exactly what the government has done, resisting at every opportunity concrete suggestions as to where the bill could be improved.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
It is important to put the bill into perspective. To do this, we have to go back a bit in history, actually to the time of confederation in 1867. Under the terms of confederation, Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia formed the confederation of Canada. Each province brought in its resources and the control over those resources.
In 1870 the three prairie provinces were transferred from a trapping and trading preserve of the Hudson's Bay Company. That took in virtually the rest of Canada except British Columbia. Those three prairie provinces became virtually a colony of the new confederation. That was not dissimilar to what is happening today with the ten provinces and it is not unlike the position the Yukon and Northwest Territories find themselves in today.
I would like to zero in on 1870, at which time Manitoba was declared a province. However, it was still de facto a colony because it could not control or own its natural resources. That was a direct result of the Riel rebellion. It does not take much to know exactly what happened at the time of the Riel rebellion.
When development of the resources was taking place, the people within that area had absolutely no say as to how they would be developed or how the environment would be protected. There was no consultation other than window dressing. We have a repeat of that in Bill C-48, particularly as it relates to the amendments under discussion and to the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
I have discussed this a number of times. I have discussed these amendments with my colleague, the member for the Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). There is dissension, there is upset in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, because we are, in fact, repeating history and treating the citizens of the Northwest Territories, be they Inuit, be they treaty Indian, be they Metis, be they white, in exactly the same way as the federal government in pre-1870 treated the province of Manitoba, and again in 1905 in the way Alberta and Saskatchewan were treated. Alberta and Saskatchewan were carved out of the colonial territories and called provinces.
We all know that the Northwest Territories and the Yukon are some day going to want to be classed as provinces, to be brought into this great country of ours as equal partners. Now is the time to start treating them that way. It was all done in 1905. The confederation of provinces at that time in 1905, when Alberta and Saskatchewan were carved out, kept the resources, if you look back to the wording, for the purposes of Canada. That is exactly what is happening today with the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. We are going to develop the resources in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories; we are going to look after all the environmental aspects; we are going to look after the rate of development. We are going to look after all those things for the good of Canada. It is all going to be done from Ottawa.
It is important to put things in perspective, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) said earlier. I

speechtext:
It was within the minister's power to do exactly that: to allow the committee to travel. The request was made; the request was denied. How do hon. members think the residents of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon feel when there is absolutely no consultation, or at best a very small window-dressing type of consultation?
The minister says that we will develop the north in harmony with the aboriginal people. How does he know it will be in harmony with the aboriginal people if he will not sit down and discuss it on their home grounds? How is it going to affect their way of life? It is going to have a dramatic effect, we all know that.
I live in the town of Fort McMurray. When I first moved there 17 years ago it was a very quiet community of somewhere around 3,000 people. Because of an impending megaproject development, the Great Canadian Oil Sands at that time, the government of the province of Alberta decided in that day to class it as a new town and to administer that new town from the city of Edmonton, from the seat of government in the province of Alberta. This is some 300 miles south of the town of Fort McMurray.
They came in with their experts from Edmonton and said, "We are going to develop your town. We are going to develop the area. We are going to be conscious of the environment. We are going to preserve your natural resources. We are going to make this a model community." We had experts; they were in the form of old-timers who had been born there or had lived there for some 30, 40 or 50 years. They were old-timers like Clare Peden, Walter Hill, Alwyn Tolen, Andy Gaudet, Mac McCormick and Alice Haxton. They were not consulted, or if they were it was window-dressing type consultation. It was not until the people in Fort McMurray decided, in their wisdom, that they were going to control their own destiny, that they were going to be taken off new town status, that they were not going to let the government control the development in the
community, that the community actually started to develop in the way that the people in Fort McMurray wanted to develop it.
I relate this only because it is exactly the same situation we are facing here today. Ministerial discretion in Bill C-48, particularly as it relates to the environment, is absolutely scary. The minister says that he is going to collaborate with the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts); he will collaborate with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc). He says, and I quote, "I will not have the authority given to other ministers that rightfully belongs to me". In other words, the minister of energy is going to become a superminister: "I am going to develop the north; I am going to do it in my way; I will consult once in a while with the minister of fisheries; I will talk to the Minister of the Environment. But it is me; I am going to take the responsibility. I will not have the authority given to the other ministers that rightfully belongs to me."
I say to the minister, Mr. Speaker, that the authority does not belong to him. The authority belongs to the people of Canada. The authority belongs to the people in the Northwest Territories. The authority for development belongs to the people in the Yukon. But true to the Liberal way of doing things-"Just watch me!" That is what we keep getting.
I go back to the minister's first statement where he said, "We spent a long time describing and defending this bill, pounding away." Then he has the audacity to come into the House and say that we have been talking about this for quite a long time and we should get it out of the House. We will get it out of the House, Mr. Minister, through you, Mr. Speaker. I suggest we will get it out of the House if he will for once listen to what the amendments say and realize what they do.
We do not wish to see the power that the minister wants for himself placed all in one hand. We would like to see this set up in a way that would be more equitable. We want to see more involvement of the residents of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. The minister said that there is compensation and that we could go through judicial channels, knowing darn well that judicial channels can take five or ten years before things can be settled. Then when the settlement is reached, the man who uses judicial channels finds a good portion of his settlement is eaten up by lawyers' fees. Surely we have enough foresight to see some of the problems that will arise. Surely we should set up a board which will judge fairly.
The minister controls the great giant, PetroCan. If a claim is made against this company, the minister hears his executives-and of course some of the executives of PetroCan are even on his own staff-telling him one thing and then he is supposed to sit there and judge and say, "Yes, you have a claim against PetroCan; we will pay it." Surely it is ludicrous to think that he can sit there and do that. Mind you, he is making himself into a superman. Perhaps he thinks he can do it, but I do not think any man could do it. There are no King Solomons, particularly in the Liberal Party.
October 15, 1981

The minister referred to the judicial process, and then he went on to say that he will hold blank cheques. He could write a blank cheque to compensate anyone he wants at any time. I say that that has shades of a pork barrel. I clearly see the opportunity of misusing this power, if he has blank cheques and people come in for compensation. I see lots of compensation before elections. Is that truly what the minister wants to be accused of later on? He is putting himself in an intolerable position. I wish the minister would heed the advice we are trying to give him.
The minister went on to say that they would carry on development in an orderly fashion in the north. By whose definition will it be in an orderly fashion? I know, it will be by the minister's definition and by the definition of the bureaucrats in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. I should like to suggest that perhaps there is another definition of orderly development, and that is that of the people living in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. The minister should go and talk with some of the people who have experienced and seen orderly development in places like Cold Lake, Bonnyville and Grand Centre where there have been projects coming in and then not coming in. That is not orderly development. That same thing will happen to the minister and his department. It was not orderly development in Fort McMurray when Great Canadian Oil Sands built their megaproject there. It became considerably more orderly when Syncrude arrived, because the local people had the autonomy to make decisions at that point in time. The local school boards had the autonomy to say that they would build schools. The local hospital boards also had autonomy. If they had to wait, as they did previously with Great Canadian Oil Sands, for a government only three hundred miles away to make the decisions, the experts and the bureaucrats could not make them. I suggest that the experts, the bureaucrats and the minister cannot make decisions for the people in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I urge the government to give consideration to the proposed amendments.

Mr. Speaker, the tragedy of Bill C-48 is being demonstrated in the debate today, that is, its effect upon the environment. We have an area which is equivalent to, or possibly larger than, the United States, but certainly larger than most nations in the world, coming under the Canada Oil and Gas Act.
In dealing with offshore, Arctic and northern resources, the federal government had an opportunity to develop a regime in those areas which would have really considered the people in the north and their desires. It would have given them an opportunity to have some say in how development proceeded and when it proceeded. It would have provided an opportunity to co-ordinate through this act co-operation among several federal government departments and provincial governments. They could have dealt with fisheries and oceans matters and the concerns of the fishermen in regard to this act. They could have had ample co-ordination with the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) in some of the areas of responsibility on which he should be speaking. Certainly in regard to northern development we would have expected that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) would have played a large role in drafting legislation which would have a tremendous impact upon northern communities and their resources. But we are dealing with an act which does not involve any co-operation between ministers. We are dealing with a bill which will put massive powers in the hands of one minister who is responsible for no one, except for the massive grab of resources in the north and off our coasts.
We should be aware of why they are in such a desperate rush for the spoils, for the oil and gas in the north and off our coasts. This is the responsibility of the government; it lies right on its head. Because of its economic and energy policies of the past, Canada finds itself in the position of a net importer of energy, dependent upon foreign oil for supplies to eastern Canada in particular. It was a policy of selling out resources in the 1950s, 1960s and early 1970s at very low prices to any buyers, without any idea of the long-term needs of Canadians in the main centres in the south or certainly any consideration of what the massive energy projects at this time would mean in the north and off our coasts. It was a sale of energy at $3 and $4 per barrel for oil to the United States until the 1970s. Then we finally realized that we were becoming short of our own

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is somewhat ironic that by tomorrow it will be one year since we engaged in this debate. We spent one hour talking about the motion of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), on October 16, 1980. It seems doubly ironic because the motion asks that a report be made public that was, in effect, already public, but was not available to the House of Commons when all farm leaders and anyone interested in the grain business had easy access to it.
I was about halfway through my comments on the report and the comments that had accompanied it when we were interrupted almost one year ago. You may recall-although I doubt that most hon. members will-that we were discussing various problems in the transportation and movement of grain from country points to the point of unloading into ocean shipping. I had pointed out that most of the recommendations of the report were either well in hand or work was going on toward them. We had gone through improvements to the
country elevator system, improvements that needed to be made with regard to co-ordination on the railroad and improvements in allocating grain.
One aspect of the report has not been completely put into place in this regard and that is basically the proposal in the Booz-Allen report to start paper pooling of rapeseed. Paper pooling has gone on with all other western grains for a good number of years. It is simply a matter of making certain that the grain that is picked up from the various elevator companies is allocated to their terminals at the other end in approximately the same ratio as it was unloaded from the elevators in the country. No one loses any grain in this way. There is the advantage of not breaking up trains into 15 or 20 pieces so that a Pioneer elevator car goes to the Pioneer terminal while three other cars go to the Saskpool terminal and seven go to the United Grain Growers terminal. Instead, the whole thing would be dumped in one terminal. They would simply keep track of how much of each grade and variety goes into the terminals and at the end of the week or month they would try to unload the trains in such a way that the amounts of grain shipped would coincide with the amounts of grain received.
That kind of agreement has not yet been worked out for rapeseed. This means extra breaking up of trains and extra time taken at the seaports because companies insist on having their own carloads of grain unloaded at their own terminal instead of working the thing out on paper.
Aside from that, most of the other recommendations of the Booz-Allen report are well in hand. I was somewhat surprised to hear the hon. member who raised the question in the first place-an issue that is now two and a half years old-direct most of his remarks to the Crow rate and the problems he thought it was causing for the railroads. I was surprised, not because I did not expect that kind of comment from the government side, but because the Booz-Allen inquiry was specifically instructed not to deal with that issue and it did not. I was surprised that the bulk of the discussion from the government side seemed to revolve around the Crow rate. It seems to me that the real reason for introducing this motion is not to gain access to a document that is, in effect, public but is, once again, to provide an opportunity to make comments about the Crow rate.
I think the understanding of the Crow rate is not as complete in eastern Canada as it might be. Without going through the history of it, I would like to point out what a present day move away from the Crow rate would do to the agricultural industry in western Canada. The examples I am going to give today will be from Alberta and this is specifically for the purpose of making the best case possible for the people interested in the Crow rate. Many groups in Alberta are now on the side of those who want to do away with the Crow because they think that in some way it will assist the economy of the province and will particularly assist livestock producers in the province.
I should like to quote from a recent issue of the "Wheat Pool 'Budget' " which is published by the Alberta Wheat Pool. An article in the December 1980 issue reads as follows:
October 15, 1981

Livestock feeders and other analysts sometimes envisage a much larger cattle and hog feeding industry if statutory rates for moving grain across Canada were eliminated. Impressive figures are often quoted reflecting supposed increase in employment, investment and value added benefits if only the Crow or statutory rate could disappear.
In Alberta ... If the Crow rate was removed and assuming that the number of cattle fed in Alberta would increase, the economic import could be measured in terms of additional barley consumed and additional packing plant activity.
Let us look at some real numbers now. The article goes on:
If the number of cattle fed increased by 10%, about 6.9 million bushels of barley would be required to feed them. The production of 51 million additional pounds of beef at a margin of $20 per hundredweight-
This was written last Christmas and now there is no margin per hundredweight.
-would provide a net benefit of $10.2 million to the feedlot operators of Alberta. If the number of cattle increased by 25%, an extra 17.2 million bushels of barley would be used and a net benefit of $25.4 million realized.
Remember that figure, Mr. Speaker; a net benefit of $25.4 million. The article goes on:
If statutory rates, however, for grain transportation disappeared, it can be assumed that the price at which feeders buy barley in Alberta would decrease by approximately the increase in the freight rate.
This must be placed in the context of the current situation where approximately 114 million bushels of barley per year are exported from Alberta. The article goes on as follows:
The 42 cents increase would apply on all of this except the additional barley utilized by feeders. In the case of 10% increase in cattle production the higher freight rate would apply on roughly 107,500,000 bushels of barley. With a 25% cattle increase, 97,200,000 bushels would be affected. This would represent a monetary loss to Alberta grain producers of $45 million and $41 million respectively.
It must be remembered that this is being compared with a $25 million gain. To this would also be added the net loss in the value of barley consumed which would amount to a loss of income of almost $60 million. So in order to realize a gain of about $25 million in Alberta, which would be the chief beneficiary of doing away with the Crow rate, farmers would need a loss of $190 million to $200 million annually. That would be the benefit of doing away with the Crow rate, Mr. Speaker! I think the recent announcement by some government ministers on October 9-
