speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to enter the debate to support the motion made by the hon. member opposite requesting a copy of the latest completed study on grain transport in western Canada. At the outset, I must confess that my interests are not directly related to the matter of western Canadian production of grain and grain movement within that area, but that my interests are of a more general character.
First and foremost is the matter of the flow of information to Members of Parliament, to which we have addressed ourselves on various occasions in this House. We have before us Bill C-43, which provides for access to information of a general character. It is unfortunate that this bill is being held
Grain Transport
in committee and is not being processed through this House. I can cast blame in the direction of my colleagues to the left in the New Democratic Party who have held that bill in committee day after day, month after month, when the people of Canada and the members of this House could have the benefit and the advantage of the information which ought to flow forward under the bill. This is just one more example: a report which could be requested-indeed, demanded-under proper access to information legislation of the kind proposed in Bill C-43.
Our concern must be broader than the particular information which is now requested to be brought before this House. We must find a general solution to the matter of the free flow of information, not only to members of this House, but to all Canadians who need and desire that kind of information. There should be no difficulty for any member of this House to support the motion, and to support the hon. member in not only requesting but demanding this report and any other information which is necessary to make intelligent assessments not only of grain transportation and production, but a great variety of other matters of interest to members of this House.
The grain industry in Canada is one which suffers from or is exposed to a high degree of government control and regulation. That is another reason for requiring the administrators of those government controls and regulations to make full and complete disclosure of what is happening in terms of the implementation of the regulations and the effect of their administration. I believe that the private sector should be given every encouragement to grow and develop in this country. I believe that it is a part and parcel of the solution to the economic woes of this country to encourage and foster the private sector in its growth and development. But as it happens, for historical reasons the grain industry has been subjected to great government control. We have organizations such as the Canadian Wheat Board, the Canadian Grain Commission and so on, all of which have an element of control over various aspects of the grain industry.
We think of western Canadian grain producers as being affected by this regulation, and we think of eastern millers as being equally affected. But there are a great many other aspects of industrial Canada which are affected by the policies applied to the grain industry in Canada. Of course, my special interest relates to the shipping industry. At first glance, one might not relate the problems of the Canadian shipping industry to this particular subject. But let me tell Your Honour, and let me make it very clear to every member of this House, that the Canadian shipping industry is very much affected by this control and regulation which is applicable to the grain industry.
By way of example, it was stated very recently that there is a threat that the Government of Canada will remove the subsidy payable in respect of the eastward transportation of grain and grain products by rail and shipped to export markets through the port of Halifax, the port of Saint John, and other east coast ports. The removal of this subsidy at this point in time would result in something like a $23 additional expense

October 15, 1981
Grain Transport
per tonne which would eventually have to be paid by the primary producers of the grain. This would also destroy a very important branch of the Canadian east coast shipping industry.
From the port of Halifax alone approximately 400,000 metric tons of grain are shipped to European and export markets. In addition, another 200,000 tonnes of flour are shipped through the port of Halifax to Cuba and beyond. I understand that flour has been purchased by the Russian government for delivery in Cuba. There is a program sponsored by the Government of Canada whereby flour is given to Third World and developing nations as a kind of gift from the Government of Canada. Much of that flour moves through the ports of Halifax and Saint John. Over 600,000 tonnes of product are moving through the port of Halifax. Just to give some idea of the magnitude of the tonne movement of grain alone, in 1980 there were 25 ship landings in the port of Halifax. In terms of revenue, even to the National Harbours Board, that is a considerable sum of money when one realizes that the wharfage charges per vessel amount to several thousand dollars. In addition, of course, there is the employment of stevedores and all the spin-offs which result from that kind of port activity.
Therefore, when the Government of Canada is considering a matter like the subsidy paid on eastern movement through east coast ports of grain and grain products, there is a broad backlash to any change in policy. It is one more piece of evidence showing how so many Canadian industries and so many Canadians are affected by government regulatory policies. Therefore, when the government says that it must cut back on government expenditures, it must recognize that the problem has been created by government involvement in the particular field in the first instance. Thus, it is not a simple matter of the saving of taxpayers' dollars. It is a matter of destroying the whole policy which has been put in place for historic reasons and which has existed for many years.
My concern in this matter of acquiring information on the grain industry and in assessing government policies which affect it and the other related industries, such as the Canadian shipping industry, is that we must be very careful and cautious because the economic result of changes in policy could be quite disastrous. If the port of Halifax, for example, were to lose that kind of grain movement of over 400,000 tonnes of grain and over 200,000 tonnes of flour, it would be a major disaster. It would result in a great deal of direct loss of employment and revenue to the port and to the Canadian shipping industry. It is with that in mind that I concern myself with this subject. But it is also of concern in the search for greater freedom in the distribution of information, not only to members of this House, but to Canadians in general.
On the Atlantic coast, and particularly in the province of Nova Scotia, we are experiencing difficult economic times. The port of Halifax this week has suffered the loss of one of the major shippers, Trans Freight Lines, which compounds the problem which has been created by the removal of Dart container lines to the port of Montreal. This is all involved in
and related to policies of the Government of Canada in the transportation field.
I hope that members on the other side can exercise more influence over the policies of the Government of Canada; and hon. members on that side should also remind themselves of their great responsibility in this area. They must assure Canadians that government policies and changes in government policies are not brought about for the benefit of one particular area or region of Canada to the detriment of another area or region of Canada. This is why we stand so often in this House and talk about the energy problem, as my friends from Alberta do, while my colleagues from the east coast talk about other government policies. We are concerned that the Government of Canada does not always recognize the adverse effect of its policies on particular areas of Canada. The east coast is a definite example. Western alienation arises from the improper application of and changes in government policies.
I want to take this opportunity to say to the government that this is one more illustration where the policies affecting grain and grain transportation can result in great harm to an area of Canada affected by changes in government policy. What we need is total disclosure of information and the opportunity to assess those government policies so that all can be assured that the policies are fair to all Canadians.
I would like to yield to some of my other colleagues who want to speak on this subject, particularly the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) who, as a western Canadian, I am sure has great concerns, just as we all do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words on this important subject this afternoon. Grain transportation is very important not only to western Canada but also to all of Canada. It is particularly important now when we have extremely high interest rates, interest rates that many of us feel are not necessary.
One of the reasons we have to suffer high interest rates, we are told, is that we have to attract foreign capital to Canada. It seems to me that rather than borrowing the money and raising interest rates to attract foreign investment, a better way would be to sell the products we are capable of producing in Canada. I would argue very strongly that one of those products is grain. If we can sell grain as well as other such products and if we had the proper kind of transportation system to get those products to export markets, that way would be better than raising interest rates. It would be much healthier for the whole economy. We would be earning dollars. Those dollars would be earned, not borrowed, and would not have to be paid back.
Grain transportation is a subject very important to western Canada, but I think all Canadians would agree that it is a subject of considerable national significance.
The government member who moved this motion is interested in producing a copy of the latest study on grain transporta-
October 15, 1981

tion. I am sure that all of us would be in favour of more government openness as far as government studies are concerned.
It is interesting to note also that we should have this subject introduced under Motion No. 4 today. It is roughly a year ago today since the co-ordinator Dr. Hugh Horner, of the Grain Transportation Authority, resigned. Since that time the government has not seen fit, nor has it had the courage, the inclination or the interest, to appoint a permanent co-ordinator to replace Dr. Horner. In fact, the Grain Transportation Authority has been without a co-ordinator for longer than it had one. That gives hon. members some idea of the importance which this government attaches to grain transportation in western Canada. As I have pointed out, it is vital and important to the whole country.
Although we are taking some time in the House today to talk about this subject, I learned this afternoon that the Department of Transport is in the process of what I think will amount to the dismantling of the Grain Transportation Authority. I learned today that a study on the effectiveness of the Grain Transportation Authority is to take place, under the direction of Mr. Tony Burgess, a member of the Grains Group. I think it is well known that he was, at best, lukewarm to the idea of a Grain Transportation Authority in the first place. It is obvious to those who have followed the success of the Grain Transportation Authority that someone who will look at it in terms of its effectiveness, who was really not in favour of it in the first place, is less likely to give it a fair hearing.
The Grain Transportation Authority has been in existence for about two years. Half of that time the Grain Transportation Authority has not had a permanent co-ordinator. Instead it has had an acting co-ordinator. If a feasibility study is to take place on the effectiveness of the Grain Transportation Authority, at least it could have been operating under a permanent co-ordinator and not an acting co-ordinator, because I think that is an unfair position in which to put the acting co-ordinator. I think also that the timing of doing an assessment on the Grain Transportation Authority is unfair because it has not been given a fair chance to operate. So I say again that I think it is ironic that the member who moved this motion is a government member. We are more concerned about grain transportation on this side because we have more members from western Canada and are the first ones affected.
Our party would be very much in favour of having all studies inquiring into grain transportation made public. We heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) announce figures on the embargo payments here two or three months ago. We were told when the embargo payments were made that we would have access to the information which the government used to decide on the level of compensation. We have seen none of those yet. Therefore, in the name of openness and freedom of information, as far as the government is concerned it should make public as many studies as possible. After all, studies are paid for by the taxpayers of Canada, and those Members of Parliament who are concerned with the
Grain Transport
wellbeing of our constituents should have access to that information to provide it to our constituents.
There are many things I could say on this matter. Grain transportation is a topic worth several days of debate in this House. The Booz-Allen report, which is not mentioned in the motion is, I gather, what the hon. member is referring to when he refers to the "latest study". It is some two or three years old now. Two Snavely reports have been issued as well as several other reports done internally on grain transportation. On several occasions we have tried to get copies of some of the work done by the Grains Group within the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and also Transport to some extent. We have been unsuccessful there. If the hon. member opposite who moved the motion could prevail on some of his colleagues on the government benches to see fit to make more than the Booz-Allen report public, we would all appreciate it and it would be to the betterment of grain transportation in western Canada.
I believe it was the member who moved the motion who spent a good deal of time on the Crow rate. Last summer quite a bit of agreement on a solution to the problems associated with the Crow rate came to pass. The Crow rate is a very complicated and touchy subject as far as many westerners are concerned, but we did see groups who were affected by the Crow in western Canada having come virtually to a consensus. They had agreed on most of the major stumbling blocks, but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stepped in and said that unless there was unanimous agreement his government was not prepared to move on a solution to the Crow rate.

Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to continue the comments I started before the dinner hour. At that time I was discussing one of the reasons for the big rush into northern and offshore energy resources. That was basically the sellout of our resources in the 1960s and early 1970s to anybody who would buy them. Now we are in the position where we must, in all haste, it seems, despite environmental concerns, rush into northern and offshore oil drilling, exploration and exploitation.
Much has been said about the silence of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). I should like to speak about the matter of fisheries now and the silence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) which is equal to that of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I would point out that Canada is currently the world's leading fish exporter, selling about $1 billion worth of fish abroad in 1980.
We have rich fishing grounds off both our eastern and western coasts. Landings by east coast fishermen in 1980 were valued at $491 million; landings off the west coast were valued at $174 million. In all, over 76,000 full and part-time fishermen depend on fishing for all or part of their income, as do another 25,000 fish plant workers. The Canadian Labour Council, in its brief to the national resources committee estimated that for every three jobs created in the fishing industry, two more are created elsewhere, and in processing, two jobs are created for each direct processing job.
In my own province of British Columbia, and on the east coast as well, sports fishing is also part of the way of life. It
October 15, 1981

provides recreation as well as being a revenue source through tourism. As well, the fishery is one of the main supports of the traditional way of life of many coastal native Indian communities. Without the fishery, which has been a part of their lives for many thousands of years, native people in my own riding of Nanaimo-Alberni and elsewhere on Canada's coasts would lose a crucial source of food and employment.
It is simply unbelievable that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has not sought greater protection for the many Canadians who need the fishery-protection from possible damage to the marine environment due to the adverse effects of oil spills, well blowouts and other damage. It is unbelievable as well that no provisions are made for adequate compensation in the event of a disasterous spill or blowout. This is particularly hard to believe in light of the knowledge we have gained in recent years about the awful consequences of such environmental emergencies.
In February, 1970, for example, the tanker Arrow sank at Chedabucto Bay near Port Hawkesbury, Nova Scotia. About 190 miles of shoreline were contaminated with oil and countless fish and shore birds were killed. It cost Canada $3 million to clean up the mess even though much of the shoreline could not be restored.
In 1978 off the coast of Brittany, the Amoco Cadiz went aground. The captain of this Liberian freighter was accused of "gross dereliction" which could not and should not be excused. This did not help the French fishermen, oystermen or lobster farmers whose livelihood was destroyed by the 64 million gallons of oil that were dumped over the 100 miles of ruined shoreline. Clean-up costs for this, the largest oil spill in history, were estimated at $600 million. Again, in March of 1979, in Cabot Strait the British oil carrier, Kurdistan, hit an iceberg, split in half, and dumped its cargo of about 29,000 tonnes of bunker oil. This spill cost $7 million to clean up. But the greatest, largest marine oil disaster that we have ever seen was not an oil spill at all; it was a well blowout in the Gulf of Mexico, the so-called Ixtoc blowout. In June of 1979, an offshore oil well owned by the Mexican Oil Corporation Pemex started spewing oil uncontrollably into the Gulf of Mexico; by the time it was capped ten months later it had spilled 140 million gallons of crude oil, some onto the coast of Texas and Louisiana. The cost of this clean-up was close to $1 billion by the time the well was capped in March of 1980. The blowout meant losses for resort owners, for Gulf shrimp fishermen and for Pemex itself.
In May of this year, a spokesman for Dome Petroleum admitted in Resolute Bay that his firm would not be able to control or clean up an oil spill in the Beaufort Sea should such a disaster take place. Yet Bill C-48 sets the stage for full speed and full-scale development of the Beaufort and other northern areas.
Again we can say that ministers entrusted with the protection of the north and its people have failed to take care of the areas entrusted to them. The Inuit people of Baffin Island say

that this amounts to little more than "cultural genocide"; their spokesman pointed out to Dome that if a spill in the sunny, warm and ice-free Gulf of Mexico could not be prevented or controlled, then there is little hope of preventing one in the often dark, cold and icy Arctic.
We should not lose sight of the concerns that have been expressed by the Ministry of the Environment concerning the chronic, creeping effluent generated by offshore drilling and exploration activities. The ministry is so concerned, in fact, that in a report issued in 1978, it says that "the long-term degradation of the world's continental shelves may not be due to catastrophic spills. It may be due to the gradual deposition of small amounts of pollutants over time." These pollutants- drill cuttings and fluids, solid industrial and domestic wastes, industrial fluid wastes and oily production water and the onshore facilities and pipelines associated with offshore works are the ones identified-are capable of devastating salt marshes, fish spawning grounds, shellfish areas and the estuaries and channels that fish need to feed and spawn in.
At the same time, the report says that most of the problems are not technical but rather "traceable to specific weaknesses in offshore drilling and production procedures and management systems." In other words, we should not blame the tools or equipment, but rather the care and consideration for the environment with which they are used. The report goes on to say that for the government, "the only adequate response is to require offshore operators to meet high standards of housekeeping and water disposal."
This bill, as it has been presented to the House, does not set such high standards. It does not, for example, establish clearly enough the definition of an oil spill; for this reason the NDP has asked for changes that would clearly state that an oil spill should be defined as any amount of 100 litres or more of oil or any other substances foreign to the environment. We should be establishing the sort of high standards of housekeeping-

It is his responsibility to be here and to appreciate the concerns of other Canadians because there are more than two Canadians in this House of Commons and in this country besides the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of the Environment. But apparently the minister has been given the task by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to attend to a more important function, and that is the matter of the Constitution. Why has the minister not been given the opportunity to voice those concerns that must be his as the Minister of the Environment, or does he care? I suggest that the entire portfolio of the Minister of the Environment is nothing more than a paper tiger. Interestingly enough, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources took exception a few moments ago to my remark that the Minister of the Environment should be interested in environmental concerns. But I see that that was passed by, as most other things are, by this government.
The amendments and the bill call for the establishment of two funds. It is very difficult to determine what these two funds intend to establish and do. Apparently $50 million or $100 million will be set aside. Perhaps the minister would like to give us his wisdom and tell us exactly how much the amount will be when he responds to the various positions that have been put forth in this connection. However, there are to be at least two funds set up, perhaps jointly funded, for the study of environmental impacts as well as for social studies. The term social studies is a very nebulous term, but it has to do with the impact the bill will have, primarily with regard to the Arctic region of Canada, which comprises some 40 per cent of the land mass.
I would suggest that this government has probably spent more money on studies and on the studious pursuit of the realities in Canada than any other government in the history of confederation. Despite the amount of money they spend on their education and their efforts to gain so-called knowledge for the benefit of their members, it is absolutely astounding that members opposite should portray themselves as such a studious group. They have to be the most inept government in the history of even their own party.
We have seen the definition in this bill of an environmental study. Again, it is nebulous. We have seen their definition of social study exercise but we have seen no reference to what they plan to do in the event that people in this country end up suffering. That is the history of that government.
Just take a look at our current situation. I could take up not only my allotted time but a full month or even a year to talk

October 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
about the government's callousness toward things like VIA Rail, mortgage rates, etc.
I would like now to turn my attention to energy. What will happen in this country if there is an oil spill, gas leak or some other catastrophic event? What they are doing is preparing themselves only for known situations.
Mr. Speaker, in the short period of time we are discussing, energy exploration is relatively new. The fact is it is minor oil spills, the mystery spills, as they are called, that are the most devastating to the people of this nation. That is the issue we should be addressing ourselves to. It is the garbage which is deposited into the sea, into our environment, which we must concern ourselves with.
I suggest that my colleagues and most of the people in this nation who make their living from the sea agree that there is very little attention paid to the mystery spills and garbage being dumped into the sea. The government has said that fishermen and other people who are adversely affected by these oil spills will be compensated in some manner through a fund yet to be determined. But no provision has yet been made. There is no particular direction given to those affected as to how they might make application to this never-never fund which is not even in existence.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if this government is truly interested in the best interests of Canadians and in Canada, as it would have us believe, it would set up a specific fund with a specified amount of money-certainly close to the amount it is prepared to spend on environmental studies-for the compensation of people whose daily lives could be adversely affected.
Mr. Speaker, it has been stated by knowledgeable people that a major oil spill in an environment which is so ecologically critical would have a tremendously adverse effect. I refer, of course, to an accident involving a tanker or a well site blowout. This government makes no provision for any compensation for people living in areas affected by such a situation.
I would like to take this opportunity to point out a matter about which the government is already totally aware. This is the proposal for an oil refinery to be erected in the State of Maine to which the province of New Brunswick has taken exception, to which I have taken exception, and to which apparently the government has taken exception. The government has stated it is prepared to pass regulations to make sure that the oil refinery in the State of Maine is not fed.
The time has come for the government to realize that it is the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) who should have a high profile in any decisions which are made that could adversely affect fisheries or any aspect of life in Canada. In order to do that, the government will have to be firm and will have to tell people in other jurisdictions that they will not be allowed to infringe upon the environment and the way of life we enjoy as Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I have a report before me which is put out by the Department of Fisheries and by Environment Canada
which is an environmental risk index for the siting of deep water oil ports. I would like to quote from that report. It says:
It is possible to build a deep water oil terminal wharf off Eastport with depths alongside in the range from 80 to 90 feet. However, entrance to such a facility is via Head Harbour Passage, which is noted for its strong tidal streams, tide rips, and whirlpools. Its narrowest point is 1,800 feet wide between the coast of Campobello Island and a 27-foot shoal. Tidal streams in this passage sometimes attain a rate of nearly five knots. At the intersection of Head Harbour Passage with Western Passage, tide rips and whirlpools are formed at certain stages of the tide.
These strong tidal streams in the narrow entrance to Eastport would make it extremely difficult, and at times impossible, to manoeuvre and berth VLCC's in this area. In fog and reduced visibility, the difficulties of navigating such vessels would be further compounded.
This has been brought to the attention of the government on many occasions. The establishment of this company in East-port, Maine, would result in the emission of half a ton of sulphur dioxide and a ton of the oxides of nitrogen and 300 pounds of particular matter into the air every hour of the day, 365 days of the year. What has been the government's response to this proposal? This response has been forthcoming from this government since 1974. It is prepared to pass a regulation, if necessary, to prohibit the passage of super tanker traffic through Head Harbour passage.
Let me bring hon. members up to date on what has transpired. The Environmental Protection Agency has been ordered to grant a permit to the Pittston people which would allow them to discharge waste water into the Bay of Fundy region. There is a referendum going on today in the town of Eastport as to whether the residents of that community want the Pittston group, which has one of the worst histories of protection of the environment on the entire North American continent. Today those people are being asked to consent to the Pittston group's moving into Eastport. The time has come for the government to act. If the government is prepared to pass a regulation, let the government pass it now. Let the government deal with matters of environmental concern. Let hon. members opposite no longer pay lip service to the fact that the environment of our Canadian children and grandchildren must be protected in the future.
This government has made no move whatsoever in that direction, and it will be a sad day indeed if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is allowed to speak for the absent Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) and for the Minister of the Environment, absent this evening, both of whom should be heard. It will be a shame, and a shame on the government if it allows that to happen! These ministers, who should know and who should have a voice respecting where environmental funds are being expended, should be involved in the decision-making process. If they are not being denied that right, then certainly the citizens of Canada, the people who make their living from the sea and the people who have to feed their families are being denied that right of being involved through their spokesmen who are supposed to represent their particular interests in this House of Commons.
October 15, 1981

1 urge hon. members present not to allow that to happen. It is the duty of every one of us who represents people who have to feed families in these days of dire plight to ensure that those people are ably and aptly represented.

Mir. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State): Mr. Speaker, to follow up on the comments of the previous speaker, I believe that it is of course important to put things back in their context. He regretted the absence of the Minister of Environment (Mr. Roberts), and at the same time tried to separate the protection offered in Bill C-48 from all other legislation aimed at protecting the environment in the Arctic and elsewhere in Canada.
Of course, the pace of northern development will accelerate, probably in spite of the gloomy prospects by our colleagues opposite and especially their former energy critic, who was under the impression that this bill would prevent his friends, the companies, from investing in the north. 1 do not think that the motions now before us bring any major surprises. I see some members of the New Democratic Party are here tonight to defend them, and I have but one regret, and that is that at the time of the vote in the committee, they were not even there to move these amendments. This is perhaps a belated reaction. I remember that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) was in a great hurry that day. He was not there to introduce his amendments, when the committee could have disposed of them one way or the other. However, the bill provides these two funds for the environment. A while ago, I heard someone say that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) had been completely ignored in this matter, and as we all know, this minister will be responsible for the environment fund north of the 60th parallel. We must also remember that all the other provisions included in the EARP and other environmental provisions still apply.
Let us look at the amendments proposed. Our colleague from the north came back earlier to the arguments which we heard during one of our trips over there, and especially with regard to the definition of a spill. I believe that he has misunderstood or else that he is becoming exclusive in his wish to overspecify, because if he excludes the general terms of the section as presently drafted and limits application of this provision to spills of over 100 litres, the bill will not protect us against smaller spills, and I do not see any advantage in having such a restrictive definition. In fact it might be a mistake, or perhaps not enough lawyers on the other side have examined this motion, but it would be completely useless to include this restriction. Frankly, I believe that it would be harmful and would prevent any control over the smaller spills that many people fear.
With Motion No. 51, even authorized spills would come within the purview of the act. Obviously, this amendment would create a legal contradiction since illegal authorized
Canada Oil and Gas Act
spills would be included. I fail to understand how something which is authorized can be illegal at the same time. This is of course a problem of semantics, and in any case to dispel the fears of hon. members opposite Section 19.2(1) will provide for a spill, whether authorized or not, which occurs offshore.
As for Motion No. 55-

It would make the person from whose work the spill resulted liable for actual loss or damage suffered by any person as a result of any such spill. He would be held responsible for what he has done, and I do not see why we need that new amendment.
Motion No. 52 provides for the reporting of authorized spills to the chief conservation officer and for the giving of notice of any such spill to the aboriginal groups affected. Such provisions could be made and would be more appropriate in regulations made in respect of authorized spills as provided for in subclause 19(4).

The motion would delete from subclause 19.2(1) the liability of a person responsible for a spill or debris for the cost and expenses reasonably incurred by the Government of Canada in acting to deal with such a spill or debris. In place of that provision, the motion would substitute a broad provision for liability, economic loss or damage resulting from spills or debris including loss of hunting, fishing and gathering opportunities of aboriginal peoples.
The provision was suggested in committee as well and, in substance, was adopted in an amendment to Clause 19, subclause 19(3). I do not have to repeat it. The version was adopted on the basis that with the addition to the existing provision on "actual loss or damage", of "loss of income and loss of hunting and gathering opportunities of aboriginal peoples," all of the essentials of the proposal would be included. The one notable exception that may be raised relates to the

Canada Oil and Gas Act
collective loss in certain circumstances, recognizing the right to bring class actions.
I do not think we are in a position to authorize that type of class action. Everyone realizes how the provinces are working on class actions. In Quebec, for example, there are bills with regard to that. I am sure the provinces will be given the opportunity to bring class actions.
As a result of the original wording in subsections (a) and (b), in cases where damage occurred in excess of the strict liability limits, there could be no additional recovery by an injured party from the negligent operator, only from any other persons who contributed to the damage. Thus, where there was negligence, and no contribution to that negligence from any other party, the injured party would be precluded from recovery above the strict liability limits. This, however, is not the intention; the new wording provides that where there is negligence, there may be recovery from any person responsible. This would include the negligent operator, subject to the strict liability provisions in subparagraph (a). Any amounts paid to the injured party as a result of subparagraph (a) would be deductible from the amount recovered on the basis of negligence, under paragraph (b) as a matter of common law.
[ Translation]
Finally, as far as Motion No. 56 is concerned-

The motion would amend the limitation provision in respect of claims under Clause 19.2. The period now provided is two years from the date on which, for example, the damage resulting from the spill occurred, but not later than six years from that date. The proposed amendment would extend the first period to the extent that the date on which the damage occurred may, in some circumstances, not be coincidental with the date on which the damage became evident.
The sense of the amendment is not unreasonable, but when the vote comes, the government will have to reflect on it.
Motion No. 57 would amend clause 19.4(1) so that the minister would be required to establish a public inquiry in every circumstance where a death, injury or danger to public safety or the environment resulted from a spill or debris or an accident related to any activity to which the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act applies.
The bill now gives the minister the discretionary authority to establish an inquiry under the Inquiries Act in circumstances such as those described above. Amending a clause in the manner proposed would unnecessarily restrict the minister's discretion. There may well be circumstances where no inquiry need be held. The proposed amendment would nevertheless require the minister to hold a hearing in every instance, and leave him open to action if he failed to do so. Indeed in that sense the amendment goes against the normal drafting convention-a lot of people like conventions these days-in that, for the above reason, such obligations are not normally placed on a minister in such circumstances.
In so far as the nature of the hearing is concerned, whether or not it is public, again the proposed amendment would
unnecessarily restrict the minister's discretion. There may well be circumstances, for example, where the nature of the inquiry to be made dictates that the hearing should be held in private in order to obtain the necessary information, or that the nature of the inquiry is such that a public hearing would be unnecessarily burdensome. Conversely, should it be appropriate, there is no reason why the minister cannot direct a public hearing under the provisions of the bill.
The motion is, in addition, somewhat inconsistent internally in that it provides that the minister must hold a hearing. However, he is not obliged to appoint qualified persons to conduct that inquiry, but may do so.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, the proposals we are debating tonight have of course been discussed at length in committee. The pros and cons have been weighed. Still I must congratulate all my colleagues of the New Democratic Party who have paid particular attention to the whole environmental question.
I am convinced that, had they had the thoughfulness and patience to wait for the votes, these amendments could have been submitted directly to the committee and we probably would have been able to negotiate some of them. I know that my colleague from Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) has done a lot of work. Indeed he is the author of several amendments in this bill and it would have been appreciated if other members had worked along that same line and with the same openness of mind.
I am convinced that the members of the Progressive Conservative Party did not have quite the same interests and perhaps not the same sensitivity. This bill may be far from perfect, of course, but I suggest that if there are abuses or if the fund turned out to be unnecessary or if there were other circumstances the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) would not hesitate to act, probably on the recommendation of his colleague the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) or of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts). Earlier someone was concerned by his absence in the House this evening. Well, we have been given the formal commitment that the Minister of the Environment would be consulted and party to all environmental problems which might crop up in the development of the Arctic. The minister's name does not appear in Bill C-48 but I think that is much more for reasons of an administrative nature than for reasons of environmental conscience.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that with this bill we will not witness another performance such as we saw in committee where hours and hours were wasted in mini-filibusters. Not only will Canadians benefit from the development of those resources but so will those who are waiting to invest and develop those regions of the country to the benefit of all the people. I hope they will not hold them hostage through Bill C-48 by saying: it has to be changed, thus trying to prevent the development of the Arctic. I know that all hon. members are anxious to see
October 15, 1981

Canada achieve self-sufficiency as soon as possible. I also know that in spite of our differences, we are all in favour of preserving our resources, but that we want a Canadian industry to develop the far north. Nobody can deny that great progress has been made as a result of this legislation; still, because it dates back some 20 years it had to be reshaped and streamlined to meet the needs of the economic reality of this day and age-in fact we are almost faced with an energy crisis-and that this bill is a cornerstone of our energy policy. We have met considerable opposition from the very beginning, especially because hon. members on the other side had no faith in our energy policy, but we had concrete results after only a few months. We have reached agreements both with Alberta and British Columbia-and we hope we will reach similar agreements with the others very soon. We were called all sorts of names- I shall forever remember that the hon. members of the Progressive Conservative Party, these self-appointed champions of Alberta, were so mean. And yet, on the night the agreement was signed, we quickly ran out of champagne because of the large number who wanted to celebrate the occasion. Perhaps the people felt that we had chosen the hard line. In connection with this bill, people are dissatisfied, but I am sure that as soon as the facts are known, there will be major finds and discoveries in the north, and that as soon as Canadians feel more secure, they will all be in favour of this bill; I suggest that the opposition would be wrong and irresponsible if merely for the sake of political gain, it delayed the passing of this bill which most Canadians are demanding, especially those who are anxious to participate in the development of the north.

speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. When I was younger than I am now, one of the things I learned from my elders and many other people was that actions speak louder than words. It seems to me Bill C-48 is one of the government actions which speaks louder than the words they have so appropriately enshrined in the constitutional package with respect to treaty and aboriginal rights. When you add Bill C-48 to the announcement of the go-ahead on the Norman Wells pipeline, when you add it to what is happening in James Bay, and when you add it to a number of other things this government is responsible for, it gives one the feeling that perhaps the celebration with which the aboriginal rights amendments in the Constitution was greeted may have been a bit premature; at least so long as the government is being run by the present party in power.

Bill C-48 is not neutral, I think, with respect to aboriginal rights or land claims. I will not say any more about it except to say I think it is intellectually dishonest to claim that any such piece of legislation can be neutral with regard to such a matter. Anything that has such an effect on a region in
Canada Oil and Gas Act
which these other things are in dispute can hardly be said to be neutral. That is simply a position not worth defending; it is indefensible.
I want to speak tonight about the question of the environment. That is what the amendments are addressing right now. I should like to say to the House Bill C-48 is an unusual, conceptual opportunity, if you will, for the House of Commons and, indeed, for the Canadian people. It is in the response of the three political parties to Bill C-48 that we can see some of the differences that exist among the three parties in the House.
Let us begin with the Progressive Conservative Party. All along they have been with the oil companies. They do not make any apology for this. They think the private sector can do a better job than the public sector; with the exception of the Conservative government in Ontario which seems to be ideologically backsliding of late. The Tories have been with the oil companies. Their major objection to Bill C-48 has been that it involves more public ownership, and it involves more involvement for Petro-Canada. They are not that concerned about the environment. There are some members of the Conservative Party who are concerned about the environment, but if they want to be intellectually honest, I think they have to realize that as long as they want to be defenders of the profit motive, they cannot at the same time be defenders of the environment. Much of the damage that has already been done to our environment has been done in the name of the profit motive; shortcuts that have been taken, technology that has not been installed, rivers that have been polluted, people that have been poisoned. All this happened because you could save money by not doing it. You could increase your profit margin by not doing it.
The Conservatives and the NDP oppose Bill C-48 fundamentally for different reasons. I want to make this clear.
Then we have the Liberals. The Liberals are moving down the road toward state capitalism, or what we might call ministerial capitalism. This bill gives all power, in heaven and earth, to the Minister of Energy (Mr. Lalonde). It does not even distribute it among other ministers in the cabinet. It gives the minister and the government more power over the corporations and more power over northerners in general. I would submit in the final analysis it gives the minister more power over northerners than it does over the corporations, because it still gives the corporations far too much of a free hand. What we are concerned with here is not just the corporations but with the people in the north who are being ignored, not only in substance but also in process, in the way this particular bill has come into being and is proceeding.
My party agrees with public ownership. We are not upset that Petro-Canada is getting more of a role to play in the development of our oil and gas resources. However, we have a different idea about what public ownership is and what it ought to mean for the Canadian people. Mr. Speaker, we want the Liberals to know we are not satisfied that Petro-Canada exists; that is not good enough. We want to see Petro-Canada simply embody a certain kind of economic development, indeed human development. It is about time we started to talk

October 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
about human development and left this narrow economic vision behind. We have a different idea of what Crown corporations are from that of the members opposite when they speak about Crown corporations and public ownership.
We want Crown corporations to be environmentally responsible. As I said before, we want them to embody a new kind of development. Because they are backed up by the wealth of the nation, and because they are backed up by the collective mandate of the Canadian people who say we want to be involved through our government in the development of these vital resources, we want them to do it in a different way. We do not want them operating at arm's length like any other business. We want them to make the kind of sound decisions that should be made. If they do not have the technology to deal with an oil spill, then let them not drill. If they do not know how to deal with certain environmental problems, then let them wait until they do.
These are the kinds of decisions that can only be made by institutions which are not in bondage to the profit motive. In that respect, we support the notion of public ownership; but we do not think it is the kind of public ownersip we are getting from the Liberal government. This distresses us. The idea of compensation, the idea that after all the seals are dead and all the fish are floating belly up someone will be compensated-is totally inadequate. There are things in this world, I would like to tell my hon. friends opposite, that there is no compensation for. He has a narrow, legalistic, individualistic view of the world which supposes that somehow people can be compensated for the general destruction of the environment which belongs to everyone. For the neglect you make possible in this bill, the whole world ought to be taking you to court. The notion of compensation will just not wash when it comes to the environment. The government will have to rethink, its categories. It will be too late by the time it gets around to it, but nevertheless it will have to do so.
Another thing we do not like about the kind of development we receive from the great Canadianizers over there is that it is development from the centre, out to and on the periphery, and it is the development of the north by people in Ottawa. It is not only state capitalism, it is state, centralized, ministerial capitalism. We believe that development in Canada needs to be more decentralized, more democratic, and needs to take more account of what the people north of 60 believe about development in their area. We believe that economic development, even if it must be public, has to respect the various northern communities, because in the final analysis a publicly-owned polluted world is no better than a privately-owned polluted world when it comes to the quality of the environment. Hon. members opposite should not think that they are making any great moral strides simply by allowing Petro-Canada certain rights north of 60. We will not be satisfied by that.
We see here a kind of frozen, arrogant vision on the part of the government at a time when Canadians are looking for leadership. They are looking for some way to be led out of the
treadmill on which they find themselves in regard to energy consumption. Instead, we find the Liberal government frantically digging up the country, trying to find and extract whatever resources they can so that they do not have to face the difficult questions of conservation and demand, so that they can meet their balance of payments because they did not develop the economy of the country correctly in the first place. They have this frozen vision. I think it is tragic. We see it in the emptiness of the answers of the government day after day. Whether they are questions on finance, energy, or whatever we ask about, we are lucky to get anything that even bears a remote resemblance to an answer.
The government is not facing the question of demand versus supply. It is not facing the question that we cannot continue to have the present kind of energy consumption and that simply finding resources in the north and getting them out as quickly as possible is a self-defeating proposition in the final analysis. We must change our way of consuming these resources, not just for our own sake but for the sake of people of the future and people around the planet who exist now. If they are to have a reasonable share of the opportunity to live abundantly, we in Canada and we in the western industrialized nations will have to come to some very, very difficult realization of where we stand with regard to energy consumption and energy growth. This is what is so empty about Bill C-48, apart from its total inadequacy vis-a-vis the environment. What is empty about it is that it does not recognize any of these realities.
I do not have much more to say, except that Bill C-48 has all kinds of power, but no purpose, no perception or perspective; it is just raw, unadulterated power. It is sort of the bare bones of what is left of the Liberal vision of Canada. I regret that this is the case. We need to begin to see, whether publicly or privately-and of course I prefer publicly-that in public ownership there is the possibility of the kind of development which cares for the future, cares for the planet and cares for everyone in the world. Until we receive that kind of public sector development from the Liberal government, the New Democratic Party will not be satisfied.

stop. It caused the greatest amount of pollution ever. There is no magic in public ownership with respect to pollution. The hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill ought to know that. Rather than rave on about public ownership, I am surprised that he did not deal with some of the worth-while amendments his colleagues put forward. -"spill" means a discharge, emission or escape of oil or gas other than one that is authorized-
In other words, if he says that it is okay and it is authorized, it is not a spill. Slop it all over the place, dump oil on everyone, it is not a spill if it is authorized. The minister said that if one drops a drop of extra oil, it is a spill, but if he authorizes it any way you fellows want to put it, that does not count.
I see the minister smiling over there. How could he conceivably suggest to the House of Commons that if he authorizes some company or some agent of a company to spill oil, dump oil, dump bunker or whatever, it is not a spill, he is not liable for it and the company is not liable for it; no one is liable for the damage? The damage may exist, the environment way be hurt, but the minister specifically says that the Crown is not liable. The Crown can authorize a spill and the Crown has no liability. Presumably the person authorized or directed to spill has no liability either. I guess the people in the riding of my colleague, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq bear the brunt of it. That is the kind of thing that happens. It is all right if the minister authorizes it. Surely the amendment proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena, with respect to Section 19.1 and the amendment with respect to the definition of "spill" must be carried, because they are sensible amendments.
The minister is in the House and after I have finished speaking, I expect him to stand up and say that he is going to ask for the unanimous consent of the House to file amendments which would be better written and better described than these. I think the drafting by my colleagues in the NDP is just
Canada Oil and Gas Act
horrible and incompetent but the minister could file amendments that would cover those problems.
I should like to deal with the question of liability for a moment. The bill is not clear enough in making an operator or concessionaire who has an oil lease or whatever from the minister, absolutely and completely liable. In the United States, when the legislation with respect to the trans-Alaska pipeline authority was proposed, it provided that all damage, no matter who caused it, no matter how it was caused, whether by negligence or otherwise, was the responsibility of the person or operator involved. In other words, it was "no fault" legislation. That is the kind of legislation we have in Ontario with respect to spills caused by those who transport oil products and the like and with respect to those who store oil products and the like.
I have a client who, by mistake, turned the wrong valve and it let out not much more than 100 litres of stuff into a small creek. He did his best to clean it up and paid a $5,000 fine in my riding of Mississauga. He did his best to stop it; it was not his fault; it was a mistake and there was no evidence of negligence. There is no fault legislation in that province, and there should be no fault legislation in this bill.
The same thing applies to the construction industry. A number of members of this House who have been involved in the construction industry know that when a man on a construction job does not wear his hard hat, the employer is fined. It does not do the employer any good to say, "I told him to wear his hard hat and I supplied him with it." It is the employer who pays the fine and who is penalized. There should be the same requirement with respect to pollution and environmental matters in the north. It should be no fault legislation and this bill does not have it.
Amendments Nos. 51 and 55, although poorly drawn, attempt to create a no fault situation and they must be supported in the event that the minister does not bring in better amendments. I challenge the minister to do something that must be done. He has a poor bill and he ought to know that and he ought to clean it up.
I want to go on now to the question of damages, Mr. Speaker. There is provision in this bill that a person be entitled to collect in a lawsuit, of all things, the actual loss or damage that he suffers. There is now an attempt by the minister in Section 19.1(3) to define actual loss or damage. 1 want to say to the House and the minister through you, sir, that the normal interpretation of actual loss or damage is what is generally known in civil courts as the kind of damage you can get in a contract lawsuit-actual, proved damages. There is an attempt in subsection (3) to broaden it but it does not broaden it properly, and the minister knows that it does not because he had the benefit of good legal counsel. It is important that this House understand that the terms "actual loss or damage" are really terms that define loss or damage to real proven losses.
Let me demonstrate, Mr. Speaker. Suppose that because of a spill in the riding of Nunatsiaq a musk ox herd is destroyed. Which person can sue for the loss of the musk ox herd? Whose herd is it? You can sue for your actual loss or damage, but

October 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
who owns the herd? Who knows who owns the herd? Maybe the Crown owns the herd or maybe the aboriginal people own the herd. Can they prove they own that herd? Under no circumstances can they, but the act says it is only a person who can sue. Which person? Can a band sue? Can a community sue? Under no circumstances, Mr. Speaker. A person can sue, but he must show that he has lost something. How does a person show he has lost something because a musk ox herd was destroyed or a herd of walrus was destroyed or a bunch of beluga whales was destroyed? How do you show that you have lost something? If you can prove that you have been hunting these particular animals and that you have lost a cash amount from the sale of their hides or whatever, and you can prove what you have sold at other times and you anticipate a loss in future years because you can no longer hunt them because they do not exist, then only you can get compensation. What about your children, then? Your children do not count. Only you can sue. You cannot sue for your children or your children's children. If the herd is wiped out the best you can get is your actual loss or damage. That is what the minister has done to the people in the north.
I say to my friends in the NDP that I am glad they brought these amendments forward-but they are not good enough. They are poorly drawn, they are incompetently drawn. I say that it is the obligation of the minister at this point to take the major amendment of the hon. member for Nunatsiaq, Motion No. 53, and redefine it to include all kinds of damage going into the future. When you destroy a place where you can gather things in the wild, when you destroy a herd, when you destroy, perhaps, the spawning ground of trout, then you have done something for which it is almost impossible to prove damage.
I was thinking about this earlier, Mr. Speaker, and I said to myself that even if you could prove damage, how would you do it? I was in Baker Lake once. The people there go fishing for lake trout. They feed them to their dogs. They toss a fish to the dogs. What do they use the dog for? They do not need a dog now because they have a skidoo, so what is the value of the dog? As a matter of fact, if there is no feed for the dog, perhaps then they would kill the dog and not have any problem. But what are their damages? A can of dog food? A bag of Kibble, or something like that? Will they have to go to the supreme court of the Northwest Territories to collect the value of a can of dog food or a bag of Kibble? That is the kind of thing that is in the concept drawn up by people in Ottawa who think that the north boundary of Canada is the Meach Lake resort and that the south boundary of Canada is the Ottawa airport. They do not understand what is going on. They suspect that because there has been some damage, one can start a lawsuit. One could start a lawsuit if it is worth taking a lawsuit and worth hiring a lawyer; but would one hire a lawyer because one does not have a fish to feed one's dog? Where are the damages? With what does one pay the lawyer, even if one does collect?

Mr. Speaker, the debate we are addressing tonight is really on a very important motion, namely Bill C-48. It is probably one of the most important bills that we have debated in this House since I have been around because it affects so many areas of our lives. It will have a dramatic effect on the north and on the offshore areas of Canada. It will have a dramatic effect on the environment of both of those areas. It will affect the future job prospects for our young people. It will affect the future of our industry, and it will affect the opportunities for our young people in Canada. More specifically than that, Bill C-48 will be affecting the northerners. It will affect those people in several ways; first of all, in terms of development, and in terms of spin-off from that development, such as transportation, jobs, and even education. This bill will really have an effect on everyone in Canada. In fact, it will affect anyone who uses oil and gas, which is virtually all Canadians.
Therefore, I should be taking pleasure in participating in this debate; but, in fact, I am finding very little pleasure in participating, probably because of the weeks that we have spent on this bill in committee. Those weeks have left a bad taste in my mouth. If Your Honour can imagine it, we are dealing with an important bill which will have such a dramatic effect on the northern parts of our country and the offshore areas, and yet the committee which has been dealing with this bill has not once travelled into the area which will be affected. I have never seen such a glaring and obvious example of a government from afar. It is the kind of thing we hear complaints about all the time. It is the kind of thing which has been reinforced in committee on this particular bill. A good number of witnesses appeared before us in committee from native groups, northern communities, northern business people, environmental groups and industry, and the list goes on and on. Each of those groups was treated the same, but the government acted a lot like the proverbial three monkeys: their
Canada Oil and Gas Act
eyes were covered and they did not want to see anything; their ears were covered, and they did not want to hear anything. The only exception to that rule was in fact, their mouths, which seemed to be open all the time and going in a number of different directions. The government clearly demonstrated its blind, unthinking, unhearing, unswerving ambition to achieve its own goals; goals which had no concern for the people who will be affected. The government demonstrated its set mind. Its mind had been made up. There was no intention of changing it. That became more and more apparent as committee time went on and on.
Therefore, as I speak tonight I have a tendency to feel that it is nothing more than an exercise in futility. Just pausing briefly, let me say that I think it is important that we look at the purposes of this bill which is so important to all of us. It is a bill which really introduces new guidelines or a new regime for oil and gas production in what is commonly called Canada lands. In other words, it is the rule books. It is the game plan. It is the whole system which will control the development of oil and gas in the Yukon, in the Northwest Territories and in the offshore areas of Canada.
The effects of this bill will be seen long into the future. We can see that it is important. It is dramatic. That is the purported purpose. But after those weeks in committee, a person begins to question what the purpose of the bill is. You begin to wonder if it is not any more than an opportunity or an attempt to crown the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) as nothing more than the emperor of the north, something to allow him to rule unfettered and undeterred the very people who will be affected, such as the northerners, the natives, the environmentalists and the business people. In fact, he is even undeterred or unfettered by his colleagues, such as the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) or the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts). Effectively, what has happened is that time spent in committee has reduced what should have been a lofty opportunity to nothing more than a simple play for power.
I want to focus for a few moments on the motions before us tonight, Nos. 4, 51, 52, 53, 55, 57 and now also Motion No. 34. All of these motions really focus on the environmental concerns in Bill C-48, and as such they are an extremely important part of this bill. The question is what kind of treatment will they receive at the hands of the government? Looking back at the committee hearings we can see that the whole debate tonight will probably fall on deaf ears.
The Minister of the Environment, who should have been keenly interested in this bill and should have been keenly and dramatically involved in its drafting and in the various elements of it, did not even appear before the committee. One begins to wonder why. Perhaps it is because emperors do not like shadows. What happened to the environmental groups which appeared before us, such as the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee? A number of those groups appeared

October 15, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
before us, but they were ignored. Their submissions were never reflected in this bill. Once again, I envision those three monkeys.
This is a crucial time in terms of the development of Canada's north and in terms of Canada's offshore. It is not a time for covered ears or covered eyes. It is a time for keen and careful listening and a time for thoughtful and careful watching. It is a time for us to discuss Canada's future. The area that we are discussing tonight is really Canada's last frontier. It is Canada's future garden of resources. It is even Canada's future breadbasket. In other words, this whole area is Canada's golden opportunity. Through Bill C-48 I think all Canadians right now are gambling a bit with our future, and we are gambling heavily on this particular part of our great country. Any time anyone gambles, the first thing one should do is look at the odds. We have to cover those odds and we have to do our best to increase our chances for success.
Today, as we look at this bill, that is exactly what we have to do at this time. We have to lay the groundwork, the footings and the foundation now for whatever will happen in Canada's frontier areas in those Canada lands. If we wait until tomorrow, or next week or next year, it will be too late. Things are beginning to happen now and now is the time when we must address these fundamental issues.
Environmental concerns really become fundamental and become key to this whole discussion and issue before us tonight. I think environmental concerns really mean the difference between two options, one is short-term development, which will benefit a few people, and the other is long-term development, which will benefit all Canadians. Obviously for all of us, the short-term option is really no option at all. What we have to strive and seek for is a long-term option. That is what we want, that is what we need, and that is what we must achieve.
To my way of thinking when one talks about the environment, there are two elements to the discussion. The first is the physical element, the second is the social element. The physical element means the land, the water, the tundra and the air; all of those things that can concretely touch the tangible aspects of the environment. The second area of the environment is the social one. That is more difficult to grasp because it affects people, such as natives, Eskimos, Indians and white men who live in the north. It affects their livelihood and their whole way of life.
This evening I want to focus primarily on the physical elements of the environment, and hopefully, if time permits, touch to a small degree on the social elements of the environment.
Last summer I travelled to Taiwan. Taiwan is an interesting country. It is a small country but it has a great many people contained in its small land mass. In fact, the whole of Taiwan is smaller than the riding I represent, yet it has a population four times that of all of Canada. In Taiwan, environmental concerns become very obvious. If you take a few acres and damage them, that damage sticks out like a sore thumb. It
becomes so obvious that anyone can see it. Therefore, concerns become much more magnified.
To contrast that, two weeks ago I travelled to Inuvik in the Northwest Territories. It seems that in the Northwest Territories you can fly for miles and miles and miles. One does not see any sign of man. There are no signs of an end to that country. As far as you can see, it seems to be water, land, water, more land and more land. To spoil a few acres in that vast area would be like dropping an ice cube in the Great Lakes. One would think that it would have virtually no effect.
Just to envision how much land we are talking about in this particular area, let me say that we are talking literally of 40 per cent of the entire area of Canada. It is a tremendously vast and unspoiled area. Just because of its size, we tend to think that we have nothing to worry about, but the truth of the matter is the vastness and seemingly endless area gives a deceptive impression. This huge area does have a very thin skin; it has a very fine ecological balance. It is slow to repair itself and it is slow to heal after it has been abused.
Now is the time for some serious listening and serious thinking. Now is the time for serious discussions concerning the environment in that area. It is now that we have to lay those plans to address the situation before it is too late. Now is the time to protect this very fragile environment.
Now I want to look briefly at the motions before us. First, let us look at Motion No. 4 which reads in part:
"spill" means an amount of 100 litres or more of oil and any other substance deemed foreign to the environment.
Obviously the purpose of that motion is very simply to define what is meant by a spill. Colleagues and other speakers before me have done a good job of demonstrating just how essential it is that we know what a spill is and that we define that particular element in this type of bill.
Motion No. 51 simply tries to differentiate between an authorized and an unauthorized spill. It wants to remove the distinction in terms of environmental damage and in terms of responsibility for that damage. I think it is obvious that damages are damages, whether they are caused by an authorized spill or by an unauthorized spill.
Motion 52 is an interesting motion. Having lived in part of Canada's north, I found it particularly interesting. It says very simply that any spills must be reported to the chief conservation officer. He must then notify as quickly as possible the aboriginal peoples who might be affected. That may seem like an unimportant amendment to many people, but what often happens in an area so far removed from its government, the bureaucracy here in Ottawa being responsible, is that the people most directly affected are the last to hear about it. I feel this amendment is essential.
Motion No. 53 expands liabilities and deals with some of the liabilities that result from a spill. It is important because it takes into account such things as livelihood, as an area where
October 15, 1981

people can glean their livelihood. That, too, is of fundamental importance when talking about an area such as the north.
Motion No. 56 is also unique to the north. It recognizes the fact that what may seem like slight damage today, may have a significant effect tomorrow. Damages which may have occurred a short time ago, or even earlier, may still be the subject of a claim.
Motion No. 57 states that the minister must launch an inquiry in the event of a spill. That is important because one of the things which became obvious while studying Bill C-48 was the massive amount of ministerial discretion provided in the bill. This motion clearly addresses that question. The minister does not have an option; he must report that spill and launch an inquiry.
All these motions are important because they attempt to address the environmental concerns in the north. They attempt to begin this new regime, game plan, on a sound and solid footing.
The question that begs an answer is whether the government will listen and for once make some real and positive changes to Bill C-48, or will it be the same as we experienced in committee?
I want to touch briefly on some of the social aspects of the environment in this part of our country. Having lived there, I know what it is like to have one's resources exploited. I know what it is like to have decisions about your environment made by bureaucrats and governments from afar. I know what it is like to lose jobs to southerners and to travel thousands of miles just to get some education. I have seen the traumas people go through to get the education they require, just to be employed in their own home towns.
This government has to recognize that these people will be dramatically affected by the provisions of Bill C-48 because of the unique northern environment. Their entire living environment is likely to change. The government has to recognize this problem and to deal with it so we may all benefit. The short term benefits for a few is not a solution for us in this particular situation. We must look for a long-term benefit for all. 1 believe that Bill C-48 is literally Canada's future. The government should carefully consider the serious impact of this bill. I hope it will listen, hear and make some meaningful changes to Bill C-48 which will have a positive effect on all Canadians.

At present there is a backlog of 4,500 pension applications which are taking up to five years to process. The pension chairman has stated that he is hamstrung by the present veterans legislation. He says that the delays will get worse. Statistics

provided by veterans organizations show a 50 per cent death rate while waiting for pensions to be processed. What is the minister going to do about this?
I received a non-answer, and no action has been taken since that time.
I would like to take a moment before I continue with the debate to congratulate the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. Campbell) on his appointment to the cabinet as Minister of Veterans Affairs. We wish him well, and I want to assure him that he will receive full co-operation from this side of the House.

I will go into some statistics as to why we cannot wait until 1983 for some action. All the minister has to do is to obtain a copy of the United States legislation whereby veterans pension applications can be processed in 90 days. If that can be done in 90 days in the United States, it can certainly be done in 90 days in Canada.
I just want to give an example of the types of letters we are receiving from constituents. I want to read from a letter I just recently received from a lady veteran in my riding who, in 1978, appealed an assessment on her pension. At that time she was told she would have to wait up to two years before she could get it. She said the following in her letter to me:
My God, I could be dead by then! Maybe this is what they want, but I certainly do not.
In September of this year, the same lady veteran received a letter from the Bureau of Pensions Advocates telling her that they might get around to giving her some kind of answer in June of 1982. That is a national disgrace. We cannot accept that, and we cannot wait until 1983 for something to be done about it.
I am sure the minister is aware that there has been a recent decision which could make thousands more Canadian veterans of the Second World War eligible for pensions. This decision was made by the War Veterans Allowance Board. This means that there could be thousands more applications in the near future. If what there is now cannot be handled, I do not know how thousands more will be handled.
The minister will have to give serious consideration to leaving the pension commission here in Ottawa. One of the problems he will have will be the moving of the pension commission to Prince Edward Island because the pension commission deals also with RCMP and Department of National Defence pension applications, so I want the minister to have a look at that.
We on this side of the House are not saying every veteran is entitled to a pension. What we are saying is that veterans are entitled to answers within a reasonable period of time, not up to five years. There are even cases in which it takes over five years before there is some type of answer to pension applications. Even by 1986 there will still be about 650,000 veterans in the country with whom to deal, so the problem will not disappear. It will get worse.
I recently received an answer to an Order Paper question which gives complete detail on this complicated procedure. I have here three pages of red tape. It is nothing but a bureaucratic blockade. I am sure it is designed strictly to give defeated Liberal candidates jobs on these boards and commissions. They are loaded with them. This is the most ridiculous blockade I have seen in my life. I suggest the minister look at this complicated procedure in his department.
My colleague from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) received a letter from the Royal Canadian Legion at Port Carling which states:
It was resolved at our last general meeting that I write you and draw to your attention the disgraceful and deplorable situation regarding war veterans pensions.
