The Royal Canadian Legion Ontario Command sent a letter to their veterans whom they assist with pension applications. They tell them not to expect any kind of answer for at least two years. Another group in Ontario is organizing under the name of The Unsatisfied Veterans' Association. I quote in part from their letter:
-we plan to recruit as many unsatisfied veterans or dependants as possible. Once we have coast to coast members, we plan to hold a nationwide protest at all DVA offices throughout the country.
Their main concern is the slow processing of veterans' claims, which is a concern right across this nation.
The McCracken inquiry certainly is not acceptable. The minister will have to take immediate action. He should get hold of the American legislation. If they can do it in 90 days, we should be able to do the same.
The minister is even being sued. I first want to say it is true that the Canadian Pension Commission is experiencing some delay in the processing of applications for disability pensions. However, I think it is fair to point out that the majority of the difficulty is at the first level only. As the hon. member is aware, this problem was addressed directly by the then acting minister of veterans affairs. I want to assure the hon. member and this House tonight that I am committed as well to providing prompt and effective service to the veterans and their dependants.
The American legislation to which the hon. member refers is fundamentally different from our Pension Act. These differences can be seen in the manner in which the veteran is treated. In Canada, the Canadian Pension Commission acts as a medical detective on behalf of the veteran and researches the medical grounds on which it bases its decisions. It tries to relate present day disabilities to the relatively short period of time of military service over 36 years ago.
Most applications received by the Canadian Pension Commission are for disabilities that are associated with aging, such as arthritis, heart, chest and back conditions or failing eyesight or hearing. The gunshot wounds and the obvious war-related injuries were dealt with years ago. The Canadian Pension Commission must research carefully each case, or risk having to turn down the veteran's application. The Canadian legislation gives the veteran the benefit of the doubt, and the Commission does an excellent job of helping veterans find the relationship between today's disability and the wartime service so that they can be considered for pension. In fact, Mr. Speaker, at the first level, 40 per cent of all claims received are approved. If we consider all stages of appeal, 54 per cent of all claims registered by the commission are approved in whole or in part. When we consider that we are dealing with events which are at least 36 years ago and are trying to relate them to present medical conditions, the difficulty becomes obvious.
The United States situation has a much younger veteran population-

MANPOWER-REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET WITH WOMEN'S OUTREACH GROUPS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am sitting here wondering when we are going to see legislation that acknowledges a debt of gratitude that all Canadians owe to those who have served them, instead of producing defensive, bureaucratic gobbledygook. Pensioners are hurting. I hope we see legislation put before us quickly.
I would like to begin by congratulating the new Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bujold). I welcome him to the late show. It is unfortunate he has to be here so late in the evening. I can assure him that we are both here because on June 16 the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), once again refused to answer very simple and basic questions. That is a habit he has. I hope he will not lead us astray this evening with a script that will again not answer my questions, and that will attempt to lead Canadians astray. This is the pattern we have noticed over the past 14 or 15 months. It would be refreshing to see a change.
On June 16, I asked the minister two simple questions. First, would he meet personally with representatives of women's Outreach groups? He replied, "My officials will meet", trying to leave the impression he would meet with them when, in fact, he did not have the courage to say, no, he would not meet them." The second part of my question was also very simple. I asked: will he guarantee to this House that the moneys available for women's Outreach programs in Canada this year will at least be equal to those of last year? We got a long song and dance. If you studied what the minister said, you would find that he will increase the bureaucracy and cut the budget of women's Outreach groups; yet he tried to leave the impression all was well. In the interim, when not one of us was here to question him, this minister, who does not make statements in the House but makes statements to the press, put out another press release. In the press release of September 17, he bragged that for Outreach there is an additional $2 million. Then come the critical words: "it is being made available." What is the difference between those words and the words "is being given to?" There is a sense of certitude about expenditures that are being given to groups. There is no sense of certitude about moneys being made available. If you listen and study the wording of this minister, you are immediately suspicious that he has got himself another headline; he has left Canadians with the impression he is providing funding to Outreach. The cautious, clever man, or the cautious, clever woman in an Outreach group, would look at those words, "is being made available," and would say, "I bet come January 1 will find another announcement of other moneys being made available." This $2 million that sits here now will not go into Outreach. I defy the parliamentary secretary to rise now and guarantee that it is going to Outreach, not to any other purpose, or is it simply available as a possibility and in one month, two months or three months will be made available to some other group for the purpose of another headline?

October 15, 1981
Adjournment Debate
In the same press release, the minister told us that he was in the process of evaluating Outreach and that when the evaluation is completed he will decide whether that $2 million will be given. Then we dig a little deeper and we find that the minister has hired a firm from his riding, as he does so many things for his riding. It takes the power of the ministry to serve all Canadians. He put it in a little chunk of Winnipeg. It is the evaluation of a Canada-wide program. Then we become suspicious that there will be a report down the road which indicates clearly to Canadians that Outreach is not so good, that the minister does not really have to take the available $2 million and give it to them, that he could take that $2 million and not spend it, or give it away someplace else. The parliamentary secretary should rise and tell me that that will not be the conclusion. He should do that clearly when his turn comes.
There is a little bit more double talk. In May the minister came to Alberta and said, "Why are you native people so upset about what we will do to Outreach?" On about May 15 he said, "Don't worry". Then on July 1, within six weeks, all employees are fired, funding is terminated and the equipment is turned back to the Crown corporation. That is the word of the minister with whom we are dealing in the House. He did not make the announcement in the House, he made it to the press. He went out and made the killing announcement to the press, not to the House where we would have a chance to question him, to bring it up in the adjournment debate.
I say to the women and the native people of Canada in Outreach, that if they look at the main estimates, this minister, in the crunch with other ministers of the Crown, lost so much money in his over-all budget that 20 per cent of the programs of that department, as we have known them, will not take place in this budget year. No matter how hard we push, he will not tell us where those cuts are occurring. We will have to read the budget with the care which is required to enable us to conclude that Outreach is one of them and that what replacements there are will simply consist of a few more bureaucrats.
I bring to the attention of the parliamentary secretary the new report of the special task force. Recommendations Nos. 13 and 109 indicate that Outreach is cost-effective and that people with special needs are helped. The minister should pay attention, increase the funding, and make it happen.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to thank my colleague from Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) for his good wishes, and I trust that the answer I will give him tonight will not prompt him to follow up with another question of this kind.
In the first part of his question, he mentioned that the minister had refused to meet with women's groups. I think it is a lot more useful to solve certain problems and to allocate more funds than to meet people without having anything specific to tell them. The hon. member says that the announcement that was made in September should have been made in the House. Unfortunately, the House resumed sitting only yesterday, so it would have been difficult for the minister to make that announcement in the House. I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the answer the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) gave in June still holds true, but I would like to add certain facts.
First of all, the Treasury Board approved the allocation of an additional $0.5 million to the Outreach program for 198182. These funds come from other commission programs and were allocated to the regions.
Secondly, despite what was said earlier, that the minister allocated the majority of funds to his province and his region, the short-term contracts which the Ontario region signed with the sponsors of Outreach projects were because of a lack of funds changed to provide for 12-month terms. Thirdly, the hon. member for Egmont mentioned the various policy options presented to the minister with regard to the Outreach program. The minister is now examining these options concurrently with the report of the Task Force on Employment Opportunities for the '80s.
Finally, the hon. member for Egmont also said that at the time the minister wanted to secure additional funds for the Outreach program. I am therefore pleased, Mr. Speaker, to advise the House that, as mentioned previously, an additional sum of $1.5 million was recently approved by cabinet and the Treasury Board for 1981-82. The minister is now-reviewing the allocation of those funds which will be used to finance existing and new projects for women and the handicapped. However, Mr. Speaker, I can assure the House that the minister hopes these additional funds will allow him to increase by a third the number of Outreach projects for women.

VIA RAIL-REQUEST THAT STANDING COMMITTEE CONSIDER MATTER OF PASSENGER TRAIN ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I had the opportunity to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) a question concerning the cutbacks he announced
October 15, 1981

in passenger rail service on July 27, to take effect on November 16, a brief month away from now. My colleagues and I thought it very important that on the first day of Parliament since the announcement, we should be front and centre in our opposition to these cutbacks. The minister avoided face to face criticism for a while by waiting until after Parliament recessed for the summer to make his announcement, but now he is going to face the music, whether he likes it or not.
Yesterday 1 asked the minister whether he would refer the cutbacks to the Transport Committee of the House of Commons and cancel them until after the committee has had a chance to pass judgment on them. Earlier, he had offered to come before the committee and explain his decision. That is not enough, Mr. Speaker; it is not what we are after. An explanation of such a stupid decision makes it no less stupid and no less regrettable. 1 am asking the Minister of Transport to refer it to the committee in such a way as to make possible the reversal of his July decision.
This decision must be reversed, Mr. Speaker, for the sake of energy conservation, for the sake of jobs, for the sake of tourism, for the sake of the future of passenger rail service and for the sake of national unity.
Mr. Speaker, since I have been in this House I have not been one to get up and play the national unity game. I do not take kindly to everyone using national unity as a blanket in which to wrap themselves and thus be saved from having to defend their arguments, while they in fact do more harm to national unity than help it. But I sincerely think that such significant cuts in western Canadian and Atlantic Canadian train service, so that new equipment can be purchased for the Quebec-Windsor corridor, is a grievous error.
Like the government in general, I guess the minister just does not realize what he is playing with when he plays with the ability of Winnipegers to go by train to Saskatoon or to Edmonton or the ability of Edmontonians to go to Vancouver directly by train.
The railroad is not only a fact, it is a symbol of Canadian togetherness. And having one man from Ottawa hacking and slicing away at our rail system, by order in council yet, without public or parliamentary input, is a grievous, grievous error indeed. It shall never be forgotten. Never! The centre shall never live down this attack on the regions. By the next election, the only thing protecting the Liberals west of Thunder Bay and in the maritime provinces will be the game laws!
Democracy demands that the cutbacks be suspended and re-examined by an informed public. If the government proceeds, then I can only assume that we are much further along the road to government by decree than I really wanted to believe. I for one will not be content until we have a fully integrated and comprehensive transportation system in which passenger rail plays a crucial role, whether it is taking campers to their cottages or tourists from sea to sea. I spoke about this
Adjournment Debate
in my first speech in this House of Commons nearly two years ago this week. I will speak out as long and as often as it takes to get through the thick skulls of the Liberal government that it had better sit up, respect and invest in passenger rail service.
I am very anxious to hear from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bockstael). He comes from Winnipeg. He has Symington Yard in his riding. However, it will not be his riding for long unless he can help persuade the government to renege on its stupid decision to make the cutbacks in VIA Rail.
